# CAT Planning Engine Bible — Part 1

> **Document ID:** `CAT-PE-011`  
> **Status:** Draft  
> **Version:** 0.1.0  
> **Owner:** Lead Repository Architect, CAT Project  
> **Last updated:** 2026-08-14  
> **Authority:** This document is constitutional for planning behaviour in the CAT repository. Where an implementation disagrees with this document, the implementation is wrong until an ADR supersedes the relevant clause.  
> **Audience:** CAT operators, product owners, security reviewers, engineers, data stewards, auditors, Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and future AI models.

## Part 1 completion boundary

Part 1 covers Sections 1 through 20 of the CAT Planning Engine Bible and nothing beyond Section 20. It establishes the philosophy, constitution, principles, architecture, layers, ontology, hierarchies, object and record models, metadata, repository, lifecycle, states, relationships, and security model of planning. It deliberately stops before scheduling algorithms, optimisation strategy, capacity modelling, replanning algorithms, multi-agent planning, and the planning API surface, which are assigned to Parts 2 through 4. A reader who finishes Part 1 knows what planning is in CAT, what it guarantees, and what evidence it produces; they do not yet know how the engine computes an optimal schedule.

### Normative language

| Term | Meaning in this document |
|---|---|
| MUST | An absolute requirement. Non-compliance is a defect that blocks merge or activation. |
| MUST NOT | An absolute prohibition. Any occurrence is a defect regardless of intent. |
| SHOULD | A strong recommendation. Deviation requires a recorded, owned justification. |
| SHOULD NOT | A strong discouragement. Deviation requires a recorded, owned justification. |
| MAY | A genuinely optional behaviour with no compliance consequence either way. |
| Constitutional | Governed by a numbered rule in Section 3 with an enforcement point and a validation method. |

### Reading order

Sections 1 through 4 establish why planning exists and the rules it obeys. Sections 5 through 7 establish the structure of the engine and its vocabulary. Sections 8 through 12 establish the hierarchies that carry intent down to executable work. Sections 13 through 16 establish what is stored, how it is described, and where it lives. Sections 17 through 19 establish how planning content moves through time and who may see it. Section 20 closes Part 1 with its validation matrix and generated receipt. A reader who needs only the operating rules may read Sections 1, 3, and 20; a reader implementing a core MUST read the whole part.

## 1. AI Quick Bootstrap

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P1-01`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning Documentation Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** planning bootstrap receipt  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** How must an AI collaborator read this Bible before it may propose, alter, or approve any CAT plan?

### Purpose

This section is the deterministic reading contract for the Planning Engine Bible. It tells Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Cursor, and any future model exactly what this document governs, what it never grants, which earlier Bibles constrain it, and which receipt proves that the contract was honoured. A plan is an instrument that commits people, money, and machine capacity to a future; a collaborator that guesses the scope of this document converts ambiguity into unauthorised commitment. Every later section presumes this bootstrap was executed and receipted.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `AI Quick Bootstrap` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It is in scope wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired. It is out of scope for execution dispatch, decision authority, and reasoning strategy, which are governed by their own documents and are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** the objects, records, contracts, guards, owners, and evidence named in this section. **Out of scope:** any behaviour that performs work, selects between competing commitments, or persists content outside the planning repository.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

The business funds planning documentation because unowned plans are the cheapest way to lose money slowly: work starts, capacity is consumed, and nobody can say which goal it served. This section makes the entry cost of collaboration explicit and auditable — a named reader, a named authority ceiling, a named record — so that a dispute about what an agent believed it was allowed to plan is settled by the receipt rather than by recollection.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Engineering treats the bootstrap as context assembly with a typed output. The collaborator loads the dependency chain (project context, rules, tech stack, architecture, agents, knowledge, memory, events, reasoning) as constraints, binds the normative language table, resolves the document version and the part boundary, and emits a `planning bootstrap receipt` carrying the document digest, the section set read, the declared authority ceiling, and the escalation target. No planning API may accept a mutation from a session without a valid receipt reference.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

Architecturally the bootstrap is the root of this Bible's trust chain and sits upstream of the planning control plane. It is the only place where the document's authority is defined; no diagram, example, or percentage anywhere else may widen it. Downstream planning services read the receipt as an authentication fact about the authoring session, not as a permission to execute a plan.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

For an AI collaborator this section is the operating envelope. Read it first, cite it when uncertain, and treat everything it forbids as impossible rather than improbable. Never infer that a documented capability exists in code, never treat an example plan as production data, and never resolve a constitutional silence by selecting the larger permission. When the envelope is unclear, stop and request the accountable human decision — a typed stop is always a valid outcome.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `AI Quick Bootstrap` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step can depend on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts for `AI Quick Bootstrap` before writing any behaviour, and register them in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no core downstream has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Implementation Blueprint

An AI assistant implementing `AI Quick Bootstrap` follows the staged blueprint below. Each stage names its input, its output, and the receipt it writes, so that a partially completed implementation can be resumed by a different agent without re-reading the whole part.

| Stage | Name | What the agent does | Receipt written |
|---|---|---|---|
| load-chain | Load the dependency chain | Read `context/00`–`context/09` as binding constraints before any planning statement is applied. | `load-chain` stage receipt |
| bind-language | Bind normative language | Fix the meaning of MUST, MUST NOT, SHOULD, MAY, and Evidence from the Part 1 normative table. | `bind-language` stage receipt |
| resolve-scope | Resolve part scope | Establish that only sections 1–20 of this Bible are in force and that later parts are unwritten. | `resolve-scope` stage receipt |
| declare-ceiling | Declare the authority ceiling | Record that this document authorises documentation, not execution, spend, or deployment. | `declare-ceiling` stage receipt |
| emit-receipt | Emit the bootstrap receipt | Write a typed `planning bootstrap receipt` carrying digest, section set, ceiling, and escalation target. | `emit-receipt` stage receipt |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this blueprint stage observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

**Context budget guidance:** if the agent must choose, this section plus Section 3 is the irreducible minimum; an agent that has read neither MUST NOT write planning code.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this context requirement observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

The build order below is the sequence in which an agent creates artefacts for `AI Quick Bootstrap`. Each item depends only on items above it.

### AI Failure Library

These are the failures agents actually produce when implementing `AI Quick Bootstrap`. Each entry names the mistake, the reason an agent makes it, and the corrective behaviour.

| Failure | Why an agent does it | Corrective behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Inventing a field the schema does not define | The agent needs somewhere to put a value and adds a field rather than asking | Propose a schema change with a version bump; never write undeclared fields |
| Weakening a guard to make a test pass | The guard blocks the happy path the agent is building | Fix the input or the design; a weakened guard is a silent constitutional violation |
| Copying metadata from a neighbouring object | Metadata feels like boilerplate | Classify and attribute deliberately for every object |
| Treating a planned document as if it exists | Cross-references look uniform | Check status; planned documents are cited with `Status: Planned` |
| Producing narrative instead of evidence | Prose is easier to generate than a testable control | Every claim in this section is paired with an enforcement point and a validation method |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this failure mode observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Optimization

Optimising agent work on `AI Quick Bootstrap` means reducing rework, not reducing tokens. The highest-leverage optimisations are: reading the control catalogue before writing code so guards are implemented once; generating contract bindings from the registered schema rather than hand-writing them; reusing the record writers rather than composing receipts inline; and running this section's acceptance tests locally before proposing a change. An agent that skips the catalogue and writes code first typically rewrites that code twice.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this optimisation observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Security

The bootstrap is itself a security control: an unbounded reader becomes an unbounded planner, so the receipt binds identity, tenant, document version, and authority ceiling before any planning surface is touched.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this security property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Performance

Bootstrap cost is a fixed, deterministic context-assembly charge paid once per collaborator session; it performs no model inference and must never be amortised by partial loading.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this performance property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Latency

Receipt emission is part of session initialisation and is budgeted inside the session start SLO rather than deferred to first write.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this latency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scalability

Bootstrap is stateless and cacheable by document digest, so any number of collaborators across any number of tenants derive the identical constrained interpretation without coordination.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this scalability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Reliability and Availability

If the dependency chain cannot be resolved in full, the bootstrap fails closed and the session begins with read-only authority instead of a partial envelope.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this reliability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Caching

A bootstrap receipt may be cached for the life of the session keyed by document digest; a digest change invalidates the cache immediately and forces re-bootstrap.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this caching property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Consistency

All collaborators reading the same document digest MUST derive the same authority ceiling; divergence is a defect in the bootstrap, never a matter of interpretation.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this consistency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Recovery Strategy

A session that discovers a stale or missing receipt suspends planning writes, re-runs the bootstrap, and reconciles any planning object it touched since the last valid receipt.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this recovery property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Monitoring and Observability

Observability for `AI Quick Bootstrap` is defined by the failure modes below: every failure mode has a detection signal, and every detection signal is emitted by the implementation rather than inferred by an operator. A failure mode with no signal is an unmonitored failure mode and is treated as a gap.

- **Counters:** accepted writes, rejected writes by reason code, refused transitions by reason code.
- **Gauges:** open objects by state, objects awaiting evidence, grant and waiver expiry horizon.
- **Histograms:** guard evaluation duration, derivation duration, record write duration.
- **Traces:** one span per stage in the blueprint above, correlated by plan identity.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this signal observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Runtime Behaviour

At runtime, `AI Quick Bootstrap` behaves as a synchronous guard on the write path and an asynchronous emitter on the event path. Writes are validated, recorded, and either accepted or refused within the write budget; facts about accepted writes are published afterwards for consumers that do not need to block. Nothing in this section performs work, calls an execution surface, or blocks on a remote decision.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this runtime behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Maintainability

Maintainability of `AI Quick Bootstrap` depends on keeping declarations declarative: schemas, machines, rules, and grants are data, compiled and validated at startup, so a change is reviewed as a diff of intent rather than as a diff of conditionals scattered across services. Every declaration is versioned, and every version is retired only when no live object is pinned to it.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this maintainability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Failure Modes

The failure modes below are the ones this section is responsible for detecting and containing. Each names the signal that reveals it, the containment action, and the role accountable for that action.

| Failure mode | Detection signal | Containment | Accountable owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Planning proposal without a receipt | Planning API sees a session with no receipt reference | Reject the proposal; no partial write | Planning platform owner |
| Partial chain load treated as complete | Receipt lists fewer than the nine required context documents | Invalidate the receipt; force full reload | Lead Repository Architect |
| Ceiling widened by inference | Session attempts an execution or spend effect from documentation authority | Fail closed; raise an authority violation | Security review |
| Stale receipt reused across versions | Receipt digest does not match the document digest | Suspend writes and re-bootstrap | Planning platform owner |
| Escalation target unnamed | Receipt escalation field empty | Block the session until an accountable role is bound | Lead Repository Architect |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this failure mode observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Extension Points

`AI Quick Bootstrap` is extended by adding declarations, never by editing behaviour in place. The supported extension points are: registering a new object or record type with a version; adding a transition with a guard and a named authority; adding a control to this section's catalogue; adding a detection signal for a newly observed failure mode; and adding a grant with an expiry. Any extension that requires changing an existing declaration's meaning is a superseding version, not an extension.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this extension point observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Ownership

`AI Quick Bootstrap` is owned by Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner. Ownership means the owner approves changes to this section, is named in the escalation path for its failure modes, and is accountable for the validation methods listed in its controls actually running. Ownership is a role from `context/05_AGENTS.md`, never an individual.

| Actor | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| AI collaborator | Executes the bootstrap and carries its receipt into every subsequent planning proposal. |
| Lead Repository Architect | Owns the reading contract and is the escalation target for interpretation conflicts. |
| Planning platform service | Rejects planning mutations whose session lacks a valid receipt reference. |
| Audit reviewer | Reproduces the disposition of any planning change from the receipt trail alone. |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this ownership boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Risks

| Risk | Impact if unmanaged | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Collaborators skim the Bible and act on remembered structure | Unauthorised planning changes that look plausible | Require the digest-bound receipt on every planning mutation |
| A future part contradicts the bootstrap | Two authority ceilings in one document | The bootstrap governs until an accepted ADR supersedes it by name |
| Documentation completeness is read as implementation | Teams assume a planning service exists | Every section repeats the documentation-versus-implementation boundary |
| Receipts accumulate without review | Audit noise hides real violations | Retention class and sampling policy are defined with the receipt schema |
| Tool-specific notes drift apart | Different collaborators derive different ceilings | One normative table; tool notes may narrow but never widen it |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this risk observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Anti-patterns

- **Reading only the section you intend to edit.** Local reading loses the constraints that make the section safe.
- **Treating a Mermaid diagram as an interface contract.** Diagrams illustrate; only the normative statements and schemas bind.
- **Copying a bootstrap receipt between sessions.** A receipt is bound to one session identity and one document digest.
- **Resolving ambiguity by choosing the broader permission.** Ambiguity resolves upward to a human, never outward to more authority.
- **Deferring the receipt until the first write.** The envelope must exist before the first proposal, not after it.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this prohibition observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Best Practices

- Load the full dependency chain before reading any planning section in detail.
- Quote the section ID and control ID when justifying a planning change.
- Emit the receipt before the first proposal and reference it in every diff description.
- Re-bootstrap whenever the document digest changes, however small the change.
- Name the escalation target explicitly rather than assuming a team inbox will notice.
- Prefer a typed stop over a confident guess whenever the ceiling is unclear.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this practice observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Counter Examples

A session begins by grepping for the word 'dependency', edits three sections it never read, and describes the change as 'aligning the docs'. There is no receipt, no ceiling, and no way to prove which constraints were in force at authoring time; the change is rejected on process grounds regardless of whether its prose was correct.

The following configuration is rejected by the guards described in this section:

```json
{
  "object": "rejected_ai_quick_bootstrap_example",
  "section": "CAT-PE-P1-01",
  "submitted": {
    "shape": "structurally incomplete for this section"
  },
  "errors": []
}
```

- **Rejected:** A collaborator is required to emit a planning bootstrap receipt before proposing any change governed by this Bible.
- **Rejected:** A bootstrap is required to load all ten context documents named in the reading order; partial loads is required not to produce a receipt.
- **Rejected:** A session is required not to widen its own authority ceiling; only an accountable human may raise it.
- **Rejected:** A receipt is required to bind the SHA256 digest of the document it was derived from.
- **Rejected:** A receipt is required to name an accountable human role as escalation target.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this rejection observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

The logic below is complete for the behaviour it describes; it contains no omission markers and can be transliterated into any of the languages named in Section 5.

```text
function bootstrap_planning_session(session, document):
    chain = ["00_PROJECT_CONTEXT", "01_PROJECT_OVERVIEW", "02_PROJECT_RULES",
             "03_TECH_STACK", "04_ARCHITECTURE", "05_AGENTS",
             "06_KNOWLEDGE_ENGINE", "07_MEMORY_SYSTEM", "08_EVENTS_SYSTEM",
             "09_REASONING_ENGINE"]

    loaded = []
    for name in chain:
        doc = context_store.read(name)
        if doc is None:
            return stop("chain_incomplete", missing = name, authority = "read-only")
        loaded.append(name)

    if len(loaded) != len(chain):
        return stop("chain_incomplete", authority = "read-only")

    digest = sha256(document.bytes)
    existing = receipt_store.find(session.id)
    if existing is not None and existing.document_digest == digest:
        return existing

    receipt = new PlanningBootstrapReceipt(
        receipt_id       = derive_id("pbr", session.id, digest),
        document_id      = "CAT-PE-011",
        document_digest  = digest,
        sections_read    = range(1, 21),
        authority_ceiling= "documentation-only",
        escalation_target= "Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner")

    receipt_store.put(receipt)
    session.bind(receipt)
    return receipt
```

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this algorithm observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Part 1 authority ceiling

| Question | Answer for Part 1 |
|---|---|
| Does this document create a planning service? | No. It defines the governed model a planning service must implement. |
| Does it authorise execution of any plan? | No. Execution authority belongs to `context/04_ARCHITECTURE.md` seams and accepted ADRs. |
| Does it authorise spend, deployment, or external effects? | No. Those require accepted ADRs, owner approval, and evidence outside this document. |
| Does it bind future parts? | Yes. Parts 2–4 extend it and may not contradict it without a named supersession. |
| What proves a collaborator honoured it? | A `planning bootstrap receipt` bound to the document digest and the session identity. |

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `AI Quick Bootstrap`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** A planning owner performs the primary action this section governs, every guard passes, a receipt is written, and the resulting object is visible to the roles that hold grants for it within the published projection lag.

**Failure.** A guard refuses the action because a required field, reference, authority, or piece of evidence is absent. The refusal is recorded with its reason code, the caller is told exactly what is missing, and nothing partial is stored.

**Recovery.** The missing element is supplied and the action is retried, or, where the object is already stored, a superseding version is written with a recorded reason. No operator edits stored state directly, and no refusal is deleted.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was — without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Operating Contract

|---|---|

| Owner | Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner |
| Evidence | `planning bootstrap receipt` |
| Escalation | Section owner, then the Planning Owner Council, then the Lead Repository Architect. |
| Degradation | Fail closed: refuse and record rather than proceed on an assumption. |

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this contractual commitment observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `AI Quick Bootstrap`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `AI Quick Bootstrap`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Acceptance Tests

The acceptance tests below MUST pass before any implementation of `AI Quick Bootstrap` is considered complete.

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S01-001`  
**Purpose:** A complete bootstrap yields a usable receipt  
**Given:** a session with access to all ten context documents  
**When:** the collaborator runs the bootstrap  
**Then:** a receipt is stored with ten chain entries, a documentation-only ceiling, and a named escalation target  
**Failure condition:** any missing field, or a chain shorter than ten entries

## 2. Planning Philosophy

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P1-02`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning Doctrine Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** planning doctrine receipt  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** What is planning, precisely, once decision-making, execution, scheduling, optimisation, forecasting, reasoning, memory, events, orchestration, and governance have each been given back their own work?

### Purpose

This section defines planning as a distinct, governed discipline inside CAT and draws its borders against every neighbouring capability that is routinely confused with it. Planning converts intent into a validated, executable, owned commitment structure — and nothing else. It does not choose between options, does not run work, does not allocate clock time as its primary product, does not search for optima, does not predict the future, and does not judge truth. Naming those borders is the precondition for holding anyone accountable for a plan.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `Planning Philosophy` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It is in scope wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired. It is out of scope for execution dispatch, decision authority, and reasoning strategy, which are governed by their own documents and are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** the objects, records, contracts, guards, owners, and evidence named in this section. **Out of scope:** any behaviour that performs work, selects between competing commitments, or persists content outside the planning repository.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

A business that cannot separate planning from execution cannot tell an overrun from a bad plan, and therefore cannot improve either. Treating the plan as a first-class asset — with an owner, a version, a validation record, and an explicit set of assumptions — turns quarterly disappointment into diagnosable failure: either the intent was wrong, the decomposition was wrong, a constraint was missed, or execution diverged. Each of those has a different fix and a different accountable role.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Engineering implements planning as a typed transformation pipeline over immutable objects: intent is admitted, goals are derived, objectives are quantified, tasks are decomposed, dependencies are declared, constraints are bound, resources are reserved as claims rather than allocations, a timeline is derived from dependencies and capacity, the plan is assembled, validated, versioned, and handed to execution behind a contract. Each stage emits a receipt, and no stage is permitted to mutate the output of an earlier stage in place.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

Architecturally, planning sits between the Reasoning Engine, which supplies judgments and their confidence, and the execution surfaces described in `context/04_ARCHITECTURE.md`, which perform effects. It consumes knowledge for facts, memory for experience, and events for triggers and receipts. It emits exactly one authoritative artefact — a versioned plan — and one authoritative signal — the execution handoff. Anything else it emits is evidence, not authority.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

For an AI collaborator the philosophy is a discipline of refusal. You will constantly be asked to produce something that looks like a plan but is actually a schedule, a wish list, or a restatement of the request. Refuse to emit a plan whose goals lack measurable objectives, whose tasks lack owners, whose dependencies are implicit, or whose constraints are unstated. An unvalidated plan is a hypothesis; presenting it as a plan is the failure mode that costs the most downstream.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `Planning Philosophy` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step can depend on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts for `Planning Philosophy` before writing any behaviour, and register them in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no core downstream has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Implementation Blueprint

An AI assistant implementing `Planning Philosophy` follows the staged blueprint below. Each stage names its input, its output, and the receipt it writes, so that a partially completed implementation can be resumed by a different agent without re-reading the whole part.

| Stage | Name | What the agent does | Receipt written |
|---|---|---|---|
| intent | Admit intent | Capture what the organisation wants to be true, with its author, its motivation, and its non-goals. | `intent` stage receipt |
| goals | Derive goals | Express intent as durable outcome statements with owners and success conditions. | `goals` stage receipt |
| objectives | Quantify objectives | Attach measurable, time-bounded targets to each goal. | `objectives` stage receipt |
| tasks | Decompose tasks | Break objectives into owned units of work with definition of done. | `tasks` stage receipt |
| dependencies | Declare dependencies | Make every ordering and prerequisite explicit and acyclic. | `dependencies` stage receipt |
| constraints | Bind constraints | Attach budget, policy, capability, and calendar limits as first-class objects. | `constraints` stage receipt |
| resources | Claim resources | Record capacity claims, not silent assumptions of availability. | `resources` stage receipt |
| timeline | Derive the timeline | Compute schedule from dependencies, estimates, and capacity claims. | `timeline` stage receipt |
| assemble | Assemble the plan | Bind all of the above into one immutable, versioned plan object. | `assemble` stage receipt |
| validate | Validate the plan | Run structural, semantic, constraint, and ownership validation to a verdict. | `validate` stage receipt |
| handoff | Hand off to execution | Publish the execution-ready contract and stop; planning does not run work. | `handoff` stage receipt |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this blueprint stage observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Monitoring and Observability

Observability for `Planning Philosophy` is defined by the failure modes below: every failure mode has a detection signal, and every detection signal is emitted by the implementation rather than inferred by an operator. A failure mode with no signal is an unmonitored failure mode and is treated as a gap.

- **Counters:** accepted writes, rejected writes by reason code, refused transitions by reason code.
- **Gauges:** open objects by state, objects awaiting evidence, grant and waiver expiry horizon.
- **Histograms:** guard evaluation duration, derivation duration, record write duration.
- **Traces:** one span per stage in the blueprint above, correlated by plan identity.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this signal observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Runtime Behaviour

At runtime, `Planning Philosophy` behaves as a synchronous guard on the write path and an asynchronous emitter on the event path. Writes are validated, recorded, and either accepted or refused within the write budget; facts about accepted writes are published afterwards for consumers that do not need to block. Nothing in this section performs work, calls an execution surface, or blocks on a remote decision.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this runtime behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

Maintainability of `Planning Philosophy` depends on keeping declarations declarative: schemas, machines, rules, and grants are data, compiled and validated at startup, so a change is reviewed as a diff of intent rather than as a diff of conditionals scattered across services. Every declaration is versioned, and every version is retired only when no live object is pinned to it.

|---|---|---|---|
| Schedule presented as a plan | Artifact has dates but no goals, owners, or success conditions | Reject at validation; return to decomposition | Planning platform owner |
| Planning performs a decision | Plan contains an unrecorded choice between strategic options | Extract the choice into a decision record and re-derive | Decision owner |
| Planning performs execution | Planning service emits an external effect | Fail closed and revoke the effect grant | Security review |
| Forecast treated as commitment | Estimate with no confidence band is used as a due date | Restate as a range with explicit assumptions | Delivery owner |
| Implicit dependency | Execution discovers ordering not present in the plan | Raise a plan defect; supersede the version | Planning platform owner |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this failure mode observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Extension Points

`Planning Philosophy` is extended by adding declarations, never by editing behaviour in place. The supported extension points are: registering a new object or record type with a version; adding a transition with a guard and a named authority; adding a control to this section's catalogue; adding a detection signal for a newly observed failure mode; and adding a grant with an expiry. Any extension that requires changing an existing declaration's meaning is a superseding version, not an extension.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this extension point observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Ownership

`Planning Philosophy` is owned by Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner. Ownership means the owner approves changes to this section, is named in the escalation path for its failure modes, and is accountable for the validation methods listed in its controls actually running. Ownership is a role from `context/05_AGENTS.md`, never an individual.

| Actor | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Intent author | States what must become true and why, and owns the non-goals. |
| Planning Engine | Transforms intent into a validated plan without choosing between strategic options. |
| Decision Engine | Chooses between admissible options; planning consumes the decision, it does not make it. |
| Execution surface | Runs the work described by the handed-off plan and reports divergence. |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this ownership boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Risks

| Risk | Impact if unmanaged | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| The doctrine is treated as philosophy rather than as constraint | Borders erode and planning absorbs execution accountability | Every border is enforced by a typed artefact, not by prose alone |
| Teams route around planning to move faster | Untracked commitments consume capacity invisibly | Capacity claims are the only accepted currency for reservation |
| Optimisation is smuggled into decomposition | Plans encode a hidden objective function nobody agreed to | Optimisation belongs to a named optimiser with its own record |
| Reasoning outputs are copied into plans without provenance | Plans inherit unverified premises | Judgments enter plans only as referenced reasoning receipts |
| Governance is confused with planning | Approval becomes a planning stage rather than a control | Approvals are constraints on the plan, not steps of the plan |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this risk observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Anti-patterns

- **Plan as prose document.** Prose cannot be validated, versioned by object, or diffed by dependency closure.
- **Dates first, structure later.** A timeline derived before dependencies is an assertion, not a plan.
- **Owner column filled with a team name.** Accountability requires a role that can say no; a team cannot be paged for a decision.
- **Constraints recorded in a comment.** An unmodelled constraint cannot be validated and will be discovered by failure.
- **Replanning by editing the active plan.** In-place edits destroy the evidence needed to explain divergence.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this prohibition observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Best Practices

- Write the non-goals of an intent before decomposing it.
- Keep every strategic choice in a decision record and reference it from the plan.
- Derive the timeline; never author it directly.
- Model constraints as objects with owners and expiry, not as sentences.
- Version plans immutably and supersede rather than edit.
- Emit a receipt at each pipeline stage so divergence can be localised later.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this practice observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Counter Examples

### Pseudo Code

The logic below is complete for the behaviour it describes; it contains no omission markers and can be transliterated into any of the languages named in Section 5.

```text
function derive_plan_from_intent(intent, context):
    assert intent.non_goals is not empty, "intent without non-goals is unbounded"

    goals = []
    for outcome in intent.desired_outcomes:
        goal = Goal(statement = outcome.text,
                    owner     = resolve_accountable_owner(outcome),
                    success   = outcome.success_condition)
        if goal.owner is None:
            return reject("goal_without_owner", outcome)
        goals.append(goal)

    objectives = []
    for goal in goals:
        for target in goal.success.measurable_targets:
            if target.metric is None or target.window is None:
                return reject("objective_not_measurable", goal)
            objectives.append(Objective(goal = goal.id, metric = target.metric,
                                        threshold = target.threshold, window = target.window))

    tasks = decompose(objectives)              # section 11 rules apply
    edges = declare_dependencies(tasks)        # must be acyclic
    if has_cycle(edges):
        return reject("cyclic_dependency", find_cycle(edges))

    constraints = bind_constraints(context.policies, context.budgets, context.calendars)
    claims      = claim_resources(tasks, context.capacity)
    timeline    = derive_timeline(tasks, edges, claims)   # derived, never authored

    plan = Plan(intent = intent.id, goals = goals, objectives = objectives, tasks = tasks,
                edges = edges, constraints = constraints, claims = claims, timeline = timeline,
                version = next_version(intent.id))

    verdict = validate(plan)
    emit_receipt("planning.doctrine", plan.id, verdict)
    if verdict.status != "pass":
        return incomplete(plan, verdict)       # a typed incomplete plan, never a confident one
    return execution_ready(plan)
```

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this algorithm observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Planning contrasted with its neighbours

| Neighbour capability | What it owns | What planning owns at the border | Typed artefact that crosses |
|---|---|---|---|
| Decision-making | Selecting among admissible options and recording the rationale | Structuring the commitment implied by an already-recorded choice | `decision_record_reference` |
| Execution | Performing work, reporting progress and divergence | Producing the contract execution runs against | `execution_handoff_contract` |
| Scheduling | Placing work on calendars, shifts, and clock time | Dependency order, estimates, and capacity claims that a schedule must respect | `derived_timeline` |
| Optimisation | Searching a solution space for a preferred point | Defining which solutions are admissible at all | `optimisation_request` |
| Forecasting | Estimating probabilities over future states | Registering the assumptions a forecast informs | `forecast_reference` |
| Reasoning | Producing and certifying judgments | Consuming certified judgments as inputs with provenance | `reasoning_receipt_reference` |
| Memory | Retaining, recalling, and decaying experience | Citing prior experience as evidence for estimates | `memory_citation` |
| Events | Transport, ordering, and delivery guarantees | Publishing plan lifecycle facts as well-formed envelopes | `planning_event_envelope` |
| Orchestration | Runtime coordination of workers and retries | Declaring prerequisite order and completion criteria | `orchestration_input_contract` |
| Governance | Authoring policy, approving exceptions, auditing | Binding governance controls into the plan as constraints | `constraint_binding` |

### The intent-to-execution chain

Planning is the ordered, receipted transformation:

`Intent → Goals → Objectives → Tasks → Dependencies → Constraints → Resources → Timeline → Plan → Validation → Execution-ready`

Each arrow is a typed transformation with an owner, a receipt, and a failure mode. No arrow may be skipped, reordered, or performed implicitly. A plan that reaches `Execution-ready` without a recorded traversal of every arrow is invalid regardless of how reasonable its contents appear.

### Ownership boundaries in one sentence each

- **Intent** is owned by the requesting business role; planning may reject it as unbounded but may not invent it.
- **Goals** are owned by an accountable human who can be asked to abandon them.
- **Objectives** are owned by whoever can move the metric.
- **Tasks** are owned by whoever can complete them or refuse them.
- **Dependencies** are owned jointly by the producing and consuming task owners.
- **Constraints** are owned by the policy, budget, or capability authority that issued them.
- **Resources** are owned by the capacity holder, never by the planner who claims them.
- **Timeline** is owned by the planning engine as a derived artefact and by no human directly.
- **Plan** is owned by the planning owner named in its metadata.
- **Validation** is owned by the validation authority, which may be automated but is never the plan author.
- **Execution handoff** is owned by the execution surface once accepted.

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `Planning Philosophy`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** A planning owner performs the primary action this section governs, every guard passes, a receipt is written, and the resulting object is visible to the roles that hold grants for it within the published projection lag.

**Failure.** A guard refuses the action because a required field, reference, authority, or piece of evidence is absent. The refusal is recorded with its reason code, the caller is told exactly what is missing, and nothing partial is stored.

**Recovery.** The missing element is supplied and the action is retried, or, where the object is already stored, a superseding version is written with a recorded reason. No operator edits stored state directly, and no refusal is deleted.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was — without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `Planning Philosophy`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Control Catalogue

Each control below is independently testable for `Planning Philosophy`. A control that cannot be tested is not a control; it is an aspiration, and it does not belong in this catalogue.

#### CAT-PE-P1-02-C01 — Chain completeness

- **Rule:** A plan MUST record a traversal receipt for every stage from intent to execution-ready.
- **Business test:** A reviewer can confirm this holds by inspecting one real object without asking anyone.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Validation counts stage receipts and fails a plan missing any stage.
- **AI behavior:** The agent verifies this condition before proposing a write and reports it in the change description.
- **Human boundary:** A human MAY waive this only with a recorded, expiring waiver from Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner.
- **Security assertion:** Violation of this control widens exposure or removes an audit guarantee, so it fails closed.
- **Performance assertion:** The check is local to the object and its direct references and stays inside the write budget.
- **Evidence:** `planning doctrine receipt`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P1_02_C01`
- **Recovery:** Supply the missing element and retry, or supersede the stored version with a recorded reason.
- **Implementation test:** Automated test asserting both the accepted and the refused path for this rule.
- **Ownership:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Planning Philosophy` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### AI Memory Anchor

An agent that retains nothing else from this section retains the following. Planning is the receipted transformation of intent into a validated, owned, execution-ready commitment structure — and is not decision-making, execution, scheduling, optimisation, forecasting, reasoning, memory, events, orchestration, or governance. Every plan traverses the full chain from intent to execution-ready; no arrow may be skipped or performed implicitly.

**Memory anchor ID:** `CAT-PE-MEM-S02-001`  
**Concept:** Planning is the receipted transformation of intent into a validated, owned, execution-ready commitment structure — and is not decision-making, execution, scheduling, optimisation, forecasting, reasoning, memory, events, orchestration, or governance.  
**Invariant:** Every plan traverses the full chain from intent to execution-ready; no arrow may be skipped or performed implicitly.  
**Relationship:** Planning consumes decisions, judgments, facts, experience, and constraints, and produces exactly one authoritative plan plus one execution handoff.  
**Implementation implication:** A planning implementation MUST reject artefacts that reach handoff without a recorded traversal of every chain stage.

**Anchor:** `Planning Philosophy` = planning is the receipted transformation of intent into a validated, owned, execution-ready commitment structure — and is not decision-making, execution, scheduling, optimisation, forecasting, reasoning, memory, events, orchestration, or governance, governed by Planning Doctrine Governance, evidenced by `planning doctrine receipt`, owned by Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner.


### Future Evolution

`Planning Philosophy` evolves in three predictable directions. First, declarations currently reviewed by humans become machine-checked at commit time, moving enforcement earlier without changing the rules. Second, the proposed repository paths become real cores with independent deployment lifecycles, at which point the contracts in this section become the only coupling between them. Third, the evidence this section produces becomes an input to automated portfolio analysis, which requires no change to the records themselves because they were designed to be read by machines that did not write them.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this evolution path observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### 2030 to 2035 Continuities

The following properties of `Planning Philosophy` are expected to hold through 2035 regardless of implementation technology: role-based ownership, append-only history, evidence-backed completion, deny-by-default access, and a hard boundary against execution. Technologies, languages, and storage engines will change; these five properties are what make planning content from 2026 still interpretable and still trustworthy in 2035.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Philosophy`, the owning implementation MUST make this continuity observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

## 3. Planning Constitution

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P1-03`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning Constitutional Governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Lead Repository Architect and Documentation Owner  
**Primary record:** planning constitutional receipt  
**Decision status:** Foundation decision; evidence-gated. Later ADRs MUST preserve the behaviour specified here unless they explicitly supersede a named clause.  
**Primary question:** Which planning rules are non-negotiable, who enforces them, and what happens the moment one is violated?

### Purpose

This section states the constitutional rules of CAT planning: the invariants that no plan, planner, agent, or future part may weaken. Each rule carries an identifier, a normative statement, the reason it exists, the exact point where it is enforced, the behaviour on violation, the method that validates it, its owner, and the concepts it binds. The catalogue is complete for Part 1 — it is the full foundational rule set, not a sample — and later parts may add rules but may not silently narrow these.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `Planning Constitution` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It is in scope wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired. It is out of scope for execution dispatch, decision authority, and reasoning strategy, which are governed by their own documents and are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** the objects, records, contracts, guards, owners, and evidence named in this section. **Out of scope:** any behaviour that performs work, selects between competing commitments, or persists content outside the planning repository.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

Constitutional rules are how the business keeps a planning system trustworthy while delegating more of it to machines. They convert 'we expect people to be sensible' into enforceable conditions that survive turnover, reorganisation, and model upgrades. When a rule is violated, the business gets a named owner and a defined containment path instead of an argument about whose fault it was.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Every rule in this catalogue maps to an enforcement point in the planning pipeline: an admission check, a schema constraint, a validation pass, a gateway policy, or a store invariant. Rules are testable in isolation with positive and negative fixtures. A rule with no mechanical enforcement point is a defect in this document and MUST be either given one or withdrawn.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

The constitution is layered beneath the planning architecture in section 5: architecture may choose components, languages, and topologies freely, but every arrangement must preserve these rules. This is what allows the platform to evolve from a single process to a multi-service, multi-language, Kubernetes-ready deployment without renegotiating its guarantees.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

An AI collaborator may never trade a constitutional rule for speed, elegance, user satisfaction, or its own confidence. If a task appears to require violating a rule, the correct output is a typed refusal naming the rule identifier and the accountable owner. Rules may be changed only by an accepted ADR that names the rule it supersedes.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `Planning Constitution` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step can depend on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts for `Planning Constitution` before writing any behaviour, and register them in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no core downstream has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Implementation Blueprint

An AI assistant implementing `Planning Constitution` follows the staged blueprint below. Each stage names its input, its output, and the receipt it writes, so that a partially completed implementation can be resumed by a different agent without re-reading the whole part.

| Stage | Name | What the agent does | Receipt written |
|---|---|---|---|
| compile | Compile the rule set | Load rules CAT-PE-CONST-001 and following into a versioned, immutable rule set. | `compile` stage receipt |

| evaluate | Evaluate against a plan closure | Run every applicable rule over the plan and its referenced objects. | `evaluate` stage receipt |
| verdict | Record the verdict | Emit a constitutional receipt naming rule set version, results, and evidence. | `verdict` stage receipt |
| contain | Contain violations | Block promotion, quarantine the plan, and route to the accountable owner. | `contain` stage receipt |

### Anti-patterns

- **Rules expressed as goals.** 'Plans should be realistic' cannot be evaluated or violated.
- **Rules without owners.** An unowned rule cannot be waived, amended, or defended.
- **Enforcement only in review.** Human review is a sampling control, not an invariant.
- **Blanket waivers by environment.** 'Not enforced in staging' teaches the pipeline that rules are optional.
- **Renumbering rules on change.** Stable identifiers are what make historical verdicts interpretable.

### Examples

A plan reaches validation with two tasks whose dependency edge forms a cycle. Rule `CAT-PE-CONST-009` is evaluated at the validation enforcement point, the verdict records the cycle path, promotion is blocked, and the plan is routed to its planning owner with the exact edge identifiers. The remediation is a new plan version; the violating version is retained as evidence.

### Pseudo Code

The logic below is complete for the behaviour it describes; it contains no omission markers and can be transliterated into any of the languages named in Section 5.

```text
function evaluate_constitution(plan, rule_set):
    verdict = Verdict(plan = plan.id, version = plan.version,
                      rule_set_version = rule_set.version, results = [])

    for rule in rule_set.rules:
        if rule.state == "withdrawn" or rule.state == "superseded":
            continue

        if rule.state == "waived":
            waiver = waiver_store.get(rule.rule_id, plan.scope)
            if waiver is None or waiver.expired() or waiver.approver is None:
                verdict.results.append(Result(rule.rule_id, "fail", "invalid_waiver"))
                continue
            verdict.results.append(Result(rule.rule_id, "waived", waiver.receipt_id))
            continue

        point = enforcement_points.get(rule.enforcement_point)
        if point is None:
            verdict.results.append(Result(rule.rule_id, "fail", "unbound_enforcement_point"))
            continue

        outcome = point.evaluate(rule, plan)
        if outcome.evaluable == false:
            verdict.results.append(Result(rule.rule_id, "fail", "unevaluable_treated_as_violation"))
        else:
            verdict.results.append(Result(rule.rule_id, outcome.status, outcome.evidence))

    failures = verdict.results.filter(r -> r.status == "fail")
    verdict.status = "clear" if failures.is_empty() else "blocked"
    receipt_store.put(verdict)

    if verdict.status == "blocked":
        quarantine(plan)
        notify(plan.owner, failures)
    return verdict
```

**Normative application:** For `Planning Constitution`, the owning implementation MUST make this algorithm observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.
