### Repository Operations

The repository exposes a closed set of operations. Anything not in this table is not available, and a caller that needs behaviour absent from the table proposes an addition rather than reaching around the contract into the store.

| Operation | Semantics | Authority | Concurrency | Record written |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `create` | Establish a new object identity at version 1 | Create grant for the object type | Fails if identity exists | `creation_receipt` |
| `read` | Return one object at a stated version or the latest | Read grant | Returns the state token with the object | Access log entry |
| `append_version` | Add a superseding version; never mutates | Write grant plus optimistic token | Compare-and-append on version number | `version_receipt` |
| `snapshot` | Materialise a labelled point-in-time image | Snapshot grant | Consistent as of a single version | `snapshot_receipt` |
| `restore` | Create a new version whose body equals a prior version | Restore grant plus owner approval | Appends; never rewinds | `restore_receipt` |
| `query` | Structured filter over projections | Read grant scoped to the projection | Eventually consistent with published lag | Access log entry |
| `search` | Ranked text and attribute search over projections | Read grant scoped to the index | Eventually consistent with published lag | Access log entry |
| `archive` | Move bodies to cold storage; retain identity and history | Retention service authority | Refused under legal hold | `archive_receipt` |
| `purge` | Remove bodies after retention with tombstone retained | Retention service plus data owner | Refused under legal hold | `purge_receipt` |

There is no `update` and no `delete`. Their absence is the design. An update is an `append_version`, and a deletion is an `archive` followed, only after the retention window, by a `purge` that leaves a tombstone. A repository that offers update and delete cannot make any promise about its own history.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this operation contract observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Transaction Boundaries

Transaction boundaries are declared per operation so that nobody has to infer them from the code. The rule is that everything an operation promises is in one transaction, and everything it merely announces happens after.

| Boundary | Inside the transaction | Outside the transaction | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Version append | Version row, state token, receipt, outbox row | Event publication, projection update, cache invalidation | The promise is durability of the version and its evidence; delivery is a separate concern with its own retries |
| Snapshot | Snapshot manifest and receipt | Body copying to snapshot storage | The manifest fixes the content; copying is idempotent and resumable |
| Restore | New version, receipt, provenance link to the source version | Notification of restore | A restore is an ordinary append with extra provenance |
| Archive | Status change, receipt, retention marker | Physical body movement | Movement is retryable; the status change must be atomic |
| Purge | Tombstone, receipt | Physical body deletion | The tombstone must exist before the body can be irrecoverable |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this transaction boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Concurrency, Locking, and Deadlock Avoidance

The repository uses optimistic concurrency by default and pessimistic locking only where a long-running operation would otherwise waste large amounts of work. The choice is declared per operation rather than chosen per call, because a mixture chosen at call sites becomes unpredictable under load.

| Operation | Strategy | Rationale | Failure mode surfaced |
|---|---|---|---|
| `append_version` | Optimistic compare-and-append | Conflicts are rare and cheap to retry after a re-read | `version_conflict` |
| Lifecycle transition | Optimistic on state token | Same as above, at phase granularity | `state_token_stale` |
| Replanning derivation | Advisory expiring lease | A five-minute derivation wasted by a conflict is expensive | `plan_lease_held` |
| Bulk reindex | Advisory lease on the projection | Two concurrent rebuilds produce inconsistent indexes | `projection_lease_held` |
| Snapshot | Read-consistent, no lock | Snapshots read a fixed version and cannot conflict | None |
| Purge | Pessimistic row lock plus dual authority | Irreversible operations do not use optimistic control | `purge_lock_unavailable` |

Deadlock is avoided by a single rule: locks and leases are acquired in the fixed order plan, then projection, then index, and never in the reverse direction. Because every lease also expires, a violated ordering degrades into a delay rather than a permanent stall.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this locking strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Audit Obligations

Every repository operation is audited, including reads. Read auditing is unusual and deliberate: planning content contains commitments, capacity, and sometimes personnel implications, and knowing who read a plan before a reorganisation is as important as knowing who wrote it.

| Audited event | Fields recorded | Retention | Who may read the audit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Write | Actor role, grant, object, version, digest, correlation, outcome | Life of the object plus seven years | Audit grant holders |
| Read | Actor role, grant, object, version read, correlation, timestamp | Two years | Audit grant holders |
| Refusal | Actor role, attempted action, reason code, correlation | Life of the object plus seven years | Audit grant holders |
| Grant change | Granting role, subject, scope, expiry | Permanent | Audit grant holders and security owner |
| Purge | Approvers, retention basis, tombstone identity | Permanent | Audit grant holders and data owner |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this audit obligation observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `Planning Repository Runtime`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** Through a normal day the repository serves reads from projections with a published lag under two seconds, accepts appends with receipts, and runs a nightly retention pass that archives eleven closed plans and refuses one under legal hold.

**Failure.** A projection rebuild produces a digest that does not match the expected value for a known version range. The projection is quarantined rather than served, queries fall back to the stream with a degraded flag, and the rebuild is repeated from the last verified checkpoint.

**Recovery.** The corrupted projection is rebuilt from the version stream and its digest matches. Because projections are pure functions of the stream, the recovery requires no judgement and no data reconciliation, only time.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was, without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Execution Stories

**Execution path.** The execution surface reads a committed plan version through the contract with an execution read grant. The read is audited. The surface receives an immutable version identified by digest, so what it executes is exactly what was committed, not whatever the latest version happens to be when it starts.

**Boundary note.** The execution story ends at the handoff contract. Planning publishes an execution-ready artefact and stops; the execution surface owns everything after that point and reports back only as events.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this execution story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Optimization Stories

**Optimization path.** Historical comparisons that replayed two hundred versions are replaced by snapshots every twenty-five versions. Comparison duration falls from twelve seconds to under one, and the version stream remains the authority; snapshots are just faster arrival.

**Boundary note.** Optimization changes how well a candidate scores against a declared objective function; it never changes who is authorised to commit. Selection between competing commitments remains a decision and is recorded as one.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this optimization story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `Planning Repository Runtime`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs, its correlation identifier, and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Extension

Part 2 extends the planning constitution established in Part 1 Section 3, which contains rules `CAT-PE-CONST-001` through `CAT-PE-CONST-024`. This section contributes exactly one new rule. It adds a runtime obligation; it does not weaken any existing rule.

**Rule ID:** `CAT-PE-CONST-028`  
**Title:** History is appended, never rewritten  
**Normative statement:** Stored planning content MUST NOT be modified or removed in place. Corrections MUST be superseding versions, removals MUST be archive followed by retention-bound purge, and every purge MUST leave a permanent tombstone.  
**Rationale:** The evidentiary value of planning content comes entirely from the guarantee that what was written cannot be quietly changed. A system that can rewrite one field can rewrite any field, and a reader who knows that cannot rely on any field.  
**Enforcement point:** Repository contract layer offers no mutation operation, and the storage adapter refuses in-place writes to version rows.  
**Violation behavior:** The operation is refused, the attempt is audited with the actor and grant, and repeated attempts raise a security alarm.  
**Validation method:** Automated test attempting in-place modification and deletion, asserting refusal and audit; digest stability test across the retention window.  
**Owner:** Planning Data Owner  
**Related Part 1 rules:** `CAT-PE-CONST-006` (append-only history) and `CAT-PE-CONST-014` (evidence retention).

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this constitutional rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Control Catalogue

Each control below is independently testable for `Planning Repository Runtime`. A control that cannot be tested is not a control; it is an aspiration, and it does not belong in this catalogue.

#### CAT-PE-P2-24-C01 — Closed operation set

- **Rule:** The repository MUST expose only the nine declared operations and MUST NOT offer update or delete.
- **Business test:** A reviewer confirms this holds by inspecting one real object of this section without asking anyone.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Contract test asserting the operation set and asserting absence of mutation endpoints.
- **AI behavior:** The agent verifies this condition before proposing a write and reports the result in the change description.
- **Human boundary:** A human MAY waive this only with a recorded, expiring waiver from Planning Data Owner.
- **Security assertion:** Violation widens exposure or removes an audit guarantee, so the check fails closed.
- **Performance assertion:** The check is local to the object and its direct references and stays inside the section write budget.
- **Evidence:** `repository operation receipt`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P2_24_C01`

#### CAT-PE-P2-24-C17 — Security property upheld

- **Rule:** The security property stated by this section MUST hold in the implementation, not only in the prose.
- **Business test:** The property is stated in the operating contract and is checkable against a running system.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Implementation asserts the property in an automated test and emits the corresponding signal. Property: Authorisation is deny-by-default and evaluated per operation, per object, and per tenant. A grant names its scope and its expiry, and an expired grant is not a weaker grant but no grant at all. Reads are audited alongside writes. Purge requires two authorities and always leaves a tombstone, so the fact that content existed cannot itself be erased.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT trade this property away for throughput or convenience.
- **Human boundary:** Planning Data Owner approves any deviation, recorded with an expiry.
- **Security assertion:** The property is part of this section's posture and fails closed when unverifiable.
- **Performance assertion:** Verification is bounded by the object under evaluation, not by portfolio size.
- **Evidence:** `repository operation receipt`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P2_24_C17`
- **Recovery:** Restore the property, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Automated property test executed in continuous integration.
- **Ownership:** Planning Data Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Planning Repository Runtime` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

Property: The version stream per object identity is strictly ordered and read-your-writes consistent for the writer. Projections are eventually consistent with a published lag. ### Acceptance Tests

The acceptance tests below MUST pass before any implementation of `Planning Repository Runtime` is considered complete.

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-001`  
**Purpose:** Update and delete are unavailable  
**Given:** A deployed repository contract  
**When:** A caller attempts an update and a delete  
**Then:** Both are refused as unsupported operations and both attempts are audited  
**Failure condition:** Either operation exists or succeeds

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-002`  
**Purpose:** Conflicting appends produce one winner and a useful refusal  
**Given:** Two writers both holding version 4 of one object  
**When:** Both append  
**Then:** One writes version 5; the other is refused with `version_conflict` carrying current version 5  
**Failure condition:** Both succeed, or the refusal omits the current version

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-003`  
**Purpose:** Version and receipt are atomic  
**Given:** An append path with a fault injected between version insert and receipt insert  
**When:** The append runs  
**Then:** Neither the version nor the receipt is visible after the fault  
**Failure condition:** A version exists with no receipt

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-004`  
**Purpose:** Projection rebuild reproduces the digest  
**Given:** A projection built incrementally over one thousand versions  
**When:** The projection is dropped and rebuilt from the stream  
**Then:** The rebuilt projection digest equals the incremental digest  
**Failure condition:** The digests differ, indicating the projection is not a pure function of the stream

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-005`  
**Purpose:** Reads are audited  
**Given:** A read grant and a plan  
**When:** Fifty reads are performed  
**Then:** Fifty audit entries exist naming the actor, grant, object, version, and correlation identifier  
**Failure condition:** Any read is unaudited

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-006`  
**Purpose:** Purge under legal hold is refused  
**Given:** An object past its retention window with a legal hold applied  
**When:** Purge is attempted with dual authority  
**Then:** The purge is refused with `legal_hold_active` and no tombstone is written  
**Failure condition:** The object is purged

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S24-007`  
**Purpose:** Tombstone precedes body deletion  
**Given:** An object eligible for purge  
**When:** The purge runs with a fault injected after the tombstone transaction  
**Then:** The tombstone exists and the bodies remain; the retry completes deletion idempotently  
**Failure condition:** Bodies are deleted with no tombstone recorded

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this acceptance test observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Checklist

- [ ] Compare-and-append implemented with the current version returned on conflict.
- [ ] Receipt and outbox writes inside the same transaction as the version.
- [ ] Projection rebuild job proven by a scheduled digest comparison.
- [ ] Read auditing enabled with a documented sampling policy if volume requires one.
- [ ] Retention job reporting objects overdue for archive or purge.
- [ ] Lock acquisition order documented and asserted in tests.

- [ ] Every reference field resolves at write time or the write is rejected.
- [ ] Every refusal path writes a record with a reason code.
- [ ] Receipts written for every stage in the blueprint.
- [ ] Detection signals emitted for every failure mode listed above.
- [ ] Deny-by-default authorisation enforced at the repository contract layer.
- [ ] Correlation identifier propagated across every stage and every emitted event.
- [ ] Idempotency key honoured on every externally triggered entry point.
- [ ] Timeout and cancellation paths exercised by test, not only by review.
- [ ] Owners and escalation roles resolve in `context/05_AGENTS.md`.

- [ ] No stored state edited directly; every correction is a superseding version.
- [ ] Refusals retained; nothing is deleted to make the timeline look cleaner.
- [ ] Recovery receipt written and linked to the originating failure signal.
- [ ] Acceptance tests for this section re-run before the core is declared healthy.

### Future Evolution

`Planning Repository Runtime` evolves in three predictable directions. First, projections become independently deployable read services fed by the same stream, which requires no contract change because they are already derived. Second, snapshots become content-addressed and shareable across environments, making historical analysis cheap. Third, storage adapters multiply for hot and cold tiers, which Section 25 already anticipates and which the contract makes invisible to callers.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this evolution path observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### 2030 to 2035 Continuities

The following properties of `Planning Repository Runtime` are expected to hold through 2035 regardless of implementation technology: role-based ownership, append-only history, evidence-backed completion, deny-by-default access, and a hard boundary against execution. Technologies, languages, and storage engines will change; these five properties are what make planning content written in 2026 still interpretable and still trustworthy in 2035. For the repository specifically, the durable property is that the version stream is authoritative and everything else is derived. Storage engines will be replaced two or three times before 2035; a stream of immutable versions with receipts can be migrated into any of them without losing its meaning.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Repository Runtime`, the owning implementation MUST make this continuity observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

**Title:** Compare-and-append write path  
**Purpose:** Show how a conflicting write is detected and what the loser receives.  
**Audience:** Engineers  
**Reading order:** The conflict check and the write are in one transaction; the refusal carries the current version.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant W as Writer
    participant K as Contract layer
    participant S as Storage
    participant A as Audit
    W->>K: append_version(object, expected=4, body)
    K->>K: authorise, validate, resolve references
    K->>S: begin transaction
    S->>S: read current version
    alt current == 4
        S->>S: insert version 5, token, receipt, outbox
        S-->>K: commit
        K->>A: audit accepted
        K-->>W: accepted(version 5, digest)
    else current == 5
        S-->>K: rollback
        K->>A: audit refused version_conflict
        K-->>W: refused(version_conflict, current=5)
    end
```

## 25. Planning Storage Model

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P2-25`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning persistence architecture  
**Human accountable owner:** Planning Data Owner  
**Primary record:** `storage model conformance receipt`  
**Decision status:** Runtime clause set; extends Part 1 without weakening it.  
**Primary question:** What must be true of any store that holds planning content, and what is merely a reasonable first implementation choice?

### Purpose

This section defines the storage model for planning content and separates what is binding from what is proposed. Its purpose is to give implementers a concrete, buildable design without elevating that design to constitutional status. The invariants here, meaning append-only version streams, co-transactional receipts, rebuildable projections, content digests, tenancy isolation, and retention with tombstones, must hold in any store. The specific engine, schema, and file layout must not become rules by accident simply because they were written down first.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `Planning Storage Model` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It applies wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired at runtime. It does not govern execution dispatch, decision authority, or reasoning strategy, which are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** the logical entity model, the normative storage invariants, a proposed relational implementation, a future distributed option, sizing assumptions, tenancy isolation, encryption and key handling, retention tiering, and the migration procedure between physical designs.

**Out of scope:** the repository operation contract, which belongs to Section 24; query language design; and the choice of a specific product, which requires a decision record rather than a clause.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

Storage decisions are where planning systems accidentally acquire permanent constraints. A business that writes its invariants separately from its schema can change vendors, move to a different cost tier, or split hot and cold data without asking whether its planning records still mean the same thing. A business that does not will discover, usually during a cost review, that its data model and its database are the same artefact.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Engineered as a logical model with ten entities and a set of invariants, plus a proposed relational realisation. Version bodies are stored as documents with content digests; indexed attributes are extracted into generated columns so that queries do not scan bodies. Receipts, outbox entries, and audit entries are separate append-only tables with their own retention tiers. Projections are ordinary tables rebuilt from the stream and are never written to directly by application code.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

The storage model sits beneath the repository contract and is invisible above it. That invisibility is the architectural point: the contract in Section 24 is what other components depend on, so the physical design can change without a single caller changing. The three-layer presentation, normative then proposed then future, is how that invisibility is kept honest.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

An agent must never infer storage details from behaviour and then depend on them. Specifically, an agent must not assume that versions are contiguous integers in one table, that projections and streams share a transaction, or that a query it can express is a query the projection supports. When an agent needs a new access pattern it proposes a projection, which is a declarative artefact, rather than a query against internal structure.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `Planning Storage Model` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step depends on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts this section names before writing behaviour, and register each in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no downstream core has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Section-specific sequencing.** Build the declarative definitions before the behaviour, and the refusal paths before the accepted paths, so the first thing that works correctly is the thing that says no.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

| Weakening a guard to make a test pass | The guard blocks the happy path the agent is building | Fix the input or the design; a weakened guard is a silent constitutional violation |
| Treating a planned document as if it exists | Cross-references look uniform | Check status; planned documents are cited with `Status: Planned` |

The highest-leverage optimisations are: extracting only genuinely queried attributes into generated columns rather than shredding whole bodies; tiering receipts and audit entries by age so hot storage holds only what is queried; snapshotting at a declared version interval to bound replay cost; and compressing cold bodies, which are immutable and therefore ideal compression candidates. An agent that skips the control catalogue and writes code first typically rewrites that code twice.

### Security

Tenancy is part of every key and every index, so a query that omits the tenant is a malformed query rather than a broad one. Bodies are encrypted at rest with keys managed outside the store, and key rotation does not require rewriting versions because envelope encryption keeps the version body immutable. Audit entries and tombstones are written to storage that the planning cores can append to but not modify.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this security property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Performance

Reads of a single version are one indexed lookup. Attribute queries hit generated columns rather than bodies. Replay cost is bounded by the snapshot interval. Write cost is one insert per entity involved in the transaction, which is four rows for a typical append and does not grow with history length.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this performance property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Latency

Hot-tier point reads target ten milliseconds, warm-tier reads one hundred, and cold-tier reads are explicitly asynchronous with a retrieval receipt rather than pretending to be interactive. Callers see the tier in the response, so a slow cold read is explicable rather than mysterious.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this latency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scalability

Partitioning is by tenant and object identity, which are both in every key. Receipts and audit entries partition by time, which matches how they are queried and how they are retired. Projections scale separately because they are rebuildable and therefore replaceable.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this scalability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Reliability and Availability

Durability requirements are stated per entity class: versions, receipts, and tombstones require synchronous durable commit; projections and caches do not, because they are rebuildable. This distinction lets the expensive guarantee apply only where losing data would be irrecoverable.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this reliability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Caching

Immutable version bodies are cached by digest with no expiry, because content addressed by its own hash cannot become stale. Everything mutable is cached only with its state token or projection lag attached, so a consumer can always tell how fresh the answer is.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this caching property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Consistency

Per object identity, version order is total and durable before acknowledgement. Across objects there is no transactional consistency, and snapshots exist precisely so that a consistent multi-object view can be requested explicitly rather than assumed silently.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this consistency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Recovery Strategy

Projections and caches are rebuilt, never repaired. Versions, receipts, and tombstones are restored from backup with digest verification, and any object whose digest does not verify is quarantined rather than served. Backups are proven by scheduled restore drills into a non-production environment.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this recovery property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Monitoring and Observability

Observability for `Planning Storage Model` is defined by its failure modes: every failure mode has a detection signal, and every detection signal is emitted by the implementation rather than inferred by an operator. A failure mode with no signal is an unmonitored failure mode and is treated as a gap.

- **Counters:** versions written, receipts written, tier movements, digest verification failures, restore drills completed.
- **Gauges:** bytes per tier, oldest unpurged object age, projection rebuild backlog, objects under legal hold.
- **Histograms:** point read duration by tier, replay duration by version distance, rebuild duration by projection.
- **Traces:** one span per blueprint stage, correlated by plan identity and correlation identifier.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this signal observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Runtime Behaviour

At runtime the storage layer receives only what the repository contract sends it. A write inserts a version row with its digest, a state token update, a receipt row, and an outbox row in one transaction. A background process moves entities between tiers by age and policy, recording each movement. A scheduled job verifies digests on a sample of stored versions and alarms on any mismatch, because silent bit rot in an immutable store is the one failure that undermines every guarantee built on top of it.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this runtime behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Maintainability

Maintainability of `Planning Storage Model` depends on keeping declarations declarative: schemas, machines, rules, and grants are data, compiled and validated at startup, so a change is reviewed as a diff of intent rather than a diff of conditionals scattered across services. Every declaration is versioned, and a version is retired only when no live object is pinned to it. 

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this maintainability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Failure Modes

The failure modes below are the ones this section is responsible for detecting and containing. Each names the signal that reveals it, the containment action, and the role accountable for that action.

| Failure mode | Detection signal | Containment | Accountable owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Digest mismatch on read | Computed digest differs from stored digest | Quarantine the version, serve from backup, alarm immediately | Planning Data Owner |
| Tenancy leak in a query | Query plan lacking a tenant predicate detected by a linter | Refuse the query at the contract layer | Planning Security Owner |
| Tier movement failure | Movement job reports an unmoved object past policy | Retry, then alarm; the object stays readable in its current tier | Planning Data Owner |
| Backup restore drill failure | Scheduled drill fails digest verification | Treat as an incident; block the next retention purge until resolved | Planning Data Owner |
| Projection rebuild exceeds window | Rebuild duration above the declared budget | Rebuild in partitions; publish degraded lag meanwhile | Planning Data Owner |
| Encryption key unavailable | Key management call fails | Refuse reads and writes of encrypted bodies; do not fall back to plaintext | Planning Security Owner |
| Storage capacity exhaustion | Free space below the declared threshold | Refuse new writes with `storage_exhausted` rather than corrupting a partial write | Planning Data Owner |
| Snapshot manifest orphaned | Manifest references a missing body | Mark the snapshot invalid; never serve a partial snapshot | Planning Data Owner |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this failure mode observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Extension Points

`Planning Storage Model` is extended by adding declarations, never by editing behaviour in place. New entity classes are added by declaring their key, immutability, durability class, and retention tier. New storage adapters are added by implementing the conformance suite. Adding an attribute to an indexed projection is a projection change, not a schema migration of stored bodies, because bodies are documents with digests rather than shredded columns. Any extension that changes an existing declaration's meaning is a superseding version, not an extension.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this extension point observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Risks

| Risk | Impact if unmanaged | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| The proposed implementation is treated as normative | A future migration is blocked because the schema became a rule | The three-layer table is part of the section; reviewers check that new clauses sit in the right layer |
| Digests are stored but never verified | Silent corruption is discovered years later during an audit | Scheduled digest verification with an alarm on any mismatch |
| Retention tiering is deferred | Hot storage cost grows until someone proposes deleting audit data | Tiering is implemented before the first production load, not after |
| Backups exist but restores are untested | The recovery plan is a hypothesis | Scheduled restore drills with digest verification, treated as failures when they fail |

### Anti-patterns

- **Shredding whole bodies into columns.** Every schema change becomes a migration of history, which is precisely what append-only storage was supposed to avoid.
- **Storing projections and streams in one transaction.** It couples rebuild to the write path and makes projections undroppable.
- **Tenancy as a filter rather than a key.** A filter can be forgotten; a key cannot.
- **Choosing a store before writing the conformance suite.** The suite then gets written to match the store, and the invariants quietly become whatever the store does.
- **Treating cold storage reads as interactive.** Callers time out, retry, and multiply the cost of an already slow path; make the asynchrony explicit.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this prohibition observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Best Practices

- Write the conformance suite first and treat it as the definition of an acceptable store.
- Keep bodies as documents with digests and extract only the attributes that are genuinely queried.
- Make tenant identity part of every key rather than every query.
- Verify digests on a schedule and alarm on the first mismatch.
- Tier receipts and audit entries by age from day one.
- Prove backups by restoring them, and treat a failed drill as an incident rather than a chore.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this practice observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Counter Examples

A team shreds plan bodies into forty normalised tables because it makes reporting convenient. Eight months later a new planning layer adds three fields. The migration rewrites every historical row, which means every historical digest changes, which means no version can be proven unmodified any more. The reporting convenience cost the system its entire evidentiary value.

The following configuration is rejected by the guards described in this section:

```json
{
  "object": "rejected_storage_model",
  "section": "CAT-PE-P2-25",
  "submitted": {
    "body_storage": "fully_shredded_normalised_tables",
    "digests": false,
    "receipts": "written_asynchronously_after_commit",
    "projections": "hand_maintained_incrementally",
    "tenancy": "filter_column_only",
    "purge": "hard_delete_no_tombstone",
    "backups": "configured_but_never_restored"
  },
  "errors": []
}
```

- **Rejected:** Bodies are required to be immutable with content digests; shredding makes every schema change a history rewrite.
- **Rejected:** Receipts are required to be co-transactional with the version they evidence, not written afterwards.
- **Rejected:** Projections are required to be rebuildable from the stream; hand-maintained projections cannot be verified.
- **Rejected:** Tenant identity is required to be part of the key, not a filter column that a query can omit.
- **Rejected:** Purge is required to leave a permanent tombstone.
- **Rejected:** Backups are required to be proven by scheduled restore drills with digest verification.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this rejection observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

The logic below is complete for the behaviour it describes; it contains no omission markers and can be transliterated into any of the languages named in Section 5.

```text
function conformance_suite(store):
    results = []

    # 1. Append-only
    id = store.create("plan", tenant="t1", body={"n": 1})
    store.append_version(id, expected=1, body={"n": 2})
    results.add("append_only", store.attempt_in_place_write(id, version=1) == refused)

    # 2. Digest present and stable
    v1 = store.read(id, version=1)
    results.add("digest_present", v1.digest is not none)
    results.add("digest_stable", v1.digest == content_digest(v1.body))

    # 3. Receipt co-transactional
    inject_fault_after("version_insert")
    outcome = store.append_version(id, expected=2, body={"n": 3})
    results.add("receipt_co_transactional",
                outcome == failed and store.current_version(id) == 2)
    clear_fault()

    # 4. Projection rebuildable
    before = store.projection_digest("plan_index")
    store.drop_projection("plan_index")
    store.rebuild_projection("plan_index")
    results.add("projection_rebuildable", store.projection_digest("plan_index") == before)

    # 5. Tenancy keyed
    results.add("tenancy_keyed", store.query_without_tenant("plan_index") == refused)

    # 6. Tombstone on purge
    store.force_retention_elapsed(id)
    store.purge(id, approvals=["data_owner", "retention_service"], basis="policy_r7")
    results.add("tombstone_permanent", store.tombstone_exists(id))
    results.add("bodies_removed", store.read(id, version=1) == not_found)

    # 7. Digest verification job detects corruption
    store.corrupt_body_for_test(id2, version=1)
    results.add("corruption_detected", store.verify_digests().contains(id2))

    return results.all_passed()

function move_tiers(policy, clock):
    for marker in retention_markers_older_than(policy.hot_days, clock):
        if marker.legal_hold: continue
        move(marker.object_id, from="hot", to="warm")
        write_receipt("tier_movement", marker, "hot->warm")
    for marker in retention_markers_older_than(policy.warm_days, clock):
        if marker.legal_hold: continue
        move(marker.object_id, from="warm", to="cold")
        write_receipt("tier_movement", marker, "warm->cold")
```

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this algorithm observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Three Layers of the Storage Model

The storage model is stated in three layers so that the binding parts stay binding when the technology changes. Only the first layer is normative. The second is a recommendation for the first implementation, and the third is an option that requires an ADR to adopt but no clause change.

| Layer | Status | What it fixes | What it deliberately leaves open |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normative architecture | Binding now | Append-only version streams per object identity, receipts co-transactional with versions, derived rebuildable projections, content digests, tenancy isolation, retention with tombstones | Every technology choice, including engine, schema layout, indexing, and file format |
| Proposed implementation | Proposed, not binding | A relational engine holding version rows, receipt rows, outbox rows, and projection tables, with JSON bodies and generated columns for indexed attributes | Which relational engine, whether projections live in the same database, and how snapshots are stored |
| Future option | Option requiring an ADR | A dedicated event store for streams, an object store for bodies and snapshots, and a search engine for projections | Whether the split is ever justified; the contract makes it invisible to callers either way |

The reason for this separation is that technology choices made early become constitutional by accident. Writing the invariants separately from the implementation means a migration is an engineering project rather than a renegotiation of what planning content means.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this layer separation observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Sizing Assumptions

Sizing is stated as an order of magnitude rather than a precise forecast, because a precise forecast made before the first user is a guess with decimal places. The purpose of these figures is to identify which dimension will hurt first.

| Dimension | Year one estimate | Growth driver | First constraint it will hit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Plan identities | Thousands | Portfolio breadth | Projection rebuild duration |
| Versions per plan | Tens | Replanning frequency | Historical comparison cost, mitigated by snapshots |
| Receipts | Hundreds of thousands | Every accepted and refused operation | Storage growth and audit query latency |
| Audit entries including reads | Millions | Read volume | Retention cost; addressed by tiering, never by disabling |
| Projection rows | Millions | Task and dependency counts | Query latency and rebuild windows |
| Snapshot manifests | Thousands | Snapshot interval policy | Object storage cost, which is the cheapest of these |

The honest conclusion from this table is that receipts and audit entries, not plans, will dominate storage. That is the correct outcome for a system whose value is its evidence, and it is why retention tiering is designed in from the start rather than added when the invoice arrives.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this sizing assumption observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Migration Between Physical Designs

Because the normative layer fixes no technology, migration between physical designs is expected at least once. The migration procedure is declared now so that it is not invented during the pressure of an actual migration.

1. Freeze the contract: no operation semantics change during a storage migration.
2. Stand up the target store and replay the version stream into it, producing digests per object.
3. Compare digests object by object; any mismatch stops the migration rather than being reconciled by hand.
4. Run both stores in parallel with the contract writing to both and reading from the source of truth.
5. Rebuild projections in the target and compare their digests with the source projections.
6. Switch reads to the target while continuing dual writes for a declared observation window.
7. Switch writes to the target, keep the source readable for the declared rollback window, then retire it.

Every step produces a receipt, and the migration itself is recorded as a decision with an approver. A migration that cannot be rolled back at step six is not ready for step six.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this migration step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `Planning Storage Model`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** The store serves hot reads in single-digit milliseconds, moves eleven closed plans to the warm tier overnight, verifies digests on a rolling sample of two thousand versions, and reports zero mismatches.

**Failure.** A digest verification finds one mismatch in a version written eleven months earlier. The version is quarantined immediately, served from backup after verification, and the incident is treated as a storage integrity failure rather than a read error.

**Recovery.** The affected version is restored from backup, its digest verified against the receipt written at the time of the original write, and the restoration is recorded. Because the receipt carried the digest independently of the body, the correct content was provable rather than assumed.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was, without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Execution Stories

**Execution path.** The execution surface reads committed bodies by digest through the contract. Because digests address immutable content, those reads are cached indefinitely and cost nothing after the first fetch, which is the one place where planning storage directly improves execution latency.

**Boundary note.** The execution story ends at the handoff contract. Planning publishes an execution-ready artefact and stops; the execution surface owns everything after that point and reports back only as events.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this execution story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Optimization Stories

**Optimization path.** Cold-tier compression of immutable bodies reduces archive storage by sixty-one percent with no change to any contract, because compression is a property of the adapter and the digest is computed over the uncompressed body.

**Boundary note.** Optimization changes how well a candidate scores against a declared objective function; it never changes who is authorised to commit. Selection between competing commitments remains a decision and is recorded as one.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this optimization story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `Planning Storage Model`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs, its correlation identifier, and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Extension

Part 2 extends the planning constitution established in Part 1 Section 3, which contains rules `CAT-PE-CONST-001` through `CAT-PE-CONST-024`. This section contributes exactly one new rule. It adds a runtime obligation; it does not weaken any existing rule.

**Rule ID:** `CAT-PE-CONST-029`  
**Title:** Invariants outlive implementations  
**Normative statement:** Storage invariants MUST be declared independently of storage technology. A specific engine, schema, or file format MUST NOT be treated as binding, and any store that passes the conformance suite MUST be an acceptable host for planning content.  
**Rationale:** Planning content must remain interpretable and provable across at least a decade, during which the underlying technology will be replaced more than once. Invariants written separately from implementations survive those replacements; invariants entangled with a schema do not.  
**Enforcement point:** The conformance suite is the acceptance gate for any storage adapter, and the three-layer presentation is enforced at review.  
**Violation behavior:** An adapter that fails the suite MUST NOT be deployed; a clause that names a product as binding is returned for relocation to the proposed layer.  
**Validation method:** Conformance suite executed against at least two engine classes before the model is considered technology-neutral in practice rather than in principle.  
**Owner:** Planning Data Owner  
**Related Part 1 rules:** `CAT-PE-CONST-006` (append-only history) and `CAT-PE-CONST-028` (history is appended, never rewritten).

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this constitutional rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Control Catalogue

Each control below is independently testable for `Planning Storage Model`. A control that cannot be tested is not a control; it is an aspiration, and it does not belong in this catalogue.

#### CAT-PE-P2-25-C01 — Technology neutrality

- **Rule:** The normative storage invariants MUST be expressible in more than one engine class, and no clause MUST name a specific product as binding.
- **Business test:** A reviewer confirms this holds by inspecting one real object of this section without asking anyone.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Review check that technology appears only in the proposed and future layers.
- **AI behavior:** The agent verifies this condition before proposing a write and reports the result in the change description.
- **Human boundary:** A human MAY waive this only with a recorded, expiring waiver from Planning Data Owner.
- **Security assertion:** Violation widens exposure or removes an audit guarantee, so the check fails closed.
- **Performance assertion:** The check is local to the object and its direct references and stays inside the section write budget.
- **Evidence:** `storage model conformance receipt`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P2_25_C01`
- **Recovery:** Supply the missing element and retry, or supersede the stored version with a recorded reason.
- **Implementation test:** Automated test asserting both the accepted path and the refused path for this rule.
- **Ownership:** Planning Data Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Planning Storage Model` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-PE-P2-25-C02 — Content digests

- **Rule:** Every stored version body MUST carry a content digest recorded independently in its receipt.
- **Business test:** A reviewer confirms this holds by inspecting one real object of this section without asking anyone.

#### CAT-PE-P2-25-C17 — Security property upheld

- **Rule:** The security property stated by this section MUST hold in the implementation, not only in the prose.
- **Business test:** The property is stated in the operating contract and is checkable against a running system.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Implementation asserts the property in an automated test and emits the corresponding signal. Property: Tenancy is part of every key and every index, so a query that omits the tenant is a malformed query rather than a broad one. Bodies are encrypted at rest with keys managed outside the store, and key rotation does not require rewriting versions because envelope encryption keeps the version body immutable. Audit entries and tombstones are written to storage that the planning cores can append to but not modify.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT trade this property away for throughput or convenience.
- **Human boundary:** Planning Data Owner approves any deviation, recorded with an expiry.
- **Security assertion:** The property is part of this section's posture and fails closed when unverifiable.

- **Evidence:** `storage model conformance receipt`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P2_25_C17`
- **Recovery:** Restore the property, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Automated property test executed in continuous integration.
- **Ownership:** Planning Data Owner
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Planning Storage Model` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

### Acceptance Tests

The acceptance tests below MUST pass before any implementation of `Planning Storage Model` is considered complete.

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-001`  
**Purpose:** Conformance suite passes on the proposed implementation  
**Given:** The proposed relational adapter  
**When:** The conformance suite runs  
**Then:** All seven conformance checks pass and the result is recorded as a receipt  
**Failure condition:** Any check fails and the adapter is still deployed

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-002`  
**Purpose:** Digest corruption is detected and quarantined  
**Given:** A stored version whose body is corrupted out of band  
**When:** The scheduled verification job runs  
**Then:** The mismatch is detected, the version quarantined, and an alarm raised naming the object and version  
**Failure condition:** The corrupted body is served

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-003`  
**Purpose:** Projection drop and rebuild reproduces the digest  
**Given:** A projection with one thousand rows built incrementally  
**When:** It is dropped and rebuilt from the stream  
**Then:** The digests match exactly  
**Failure condition:** The digests differ

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-004`  
**Purpose:** Query without a tenant is refused  
**Given:** A projection containing two tenants  
**When:** A query omitting the tenant predicate is issued  
**Then:** The query is refused at the contract layer and audited  
**Failure condition:** Rows from more than one tenant are returned

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-005`  
**Purpose:** Failed restore drill blocks purge  
**Given:** A restore drill that fails digest verification  
**When:** The scheduled purge job runs  
**Then:** The purge is skipped with the reason `restore_drill_failed` and an alarm is raised  
**Failure condition:** Purge proceeds despite an unproven backup

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S25-006`  
**Purpose:** Tier movement preserves digests  
**Given:** An object moved from hot to warm to cold  
**When:** Its digest is verified at each tier  
**Then:** The digest is identical at every tier and each movement wrote a receipt  
**Failure condition:** A digest changes during movement, or a movement is unrecorded

**Normative application:** For `Planning Storage Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this acceptance test observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

Technologies, languages, and storage engines will change; these five properties are what make planning content written in 2026 still interpretable and still trustworthy in 2035. For the storage model specifically, the durable property is the content digest. ## 26. Planning Scheduling

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P2-26`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning temporal allocation governance  
**Human accountable owner:** Planning Scheduling Owner  
**Primary record:** `scheduling run receipt`  
**Decision status:** Runtime clause set; extends Part 1 without weakening it.  
**Primary question:** What must be true of every schedule the engine produces, independent of the algorithm that produced it?

### Purpose

This section defines scheduling as a governed, reproducible function rather than an algorithm. It fixes the invariants every schedule must satisfy, the complete set of declared inputs, the treatment of work that cannot be scheduled, the recognised algorithm classes and their degradation behaviour, and the receipts that make a schedule explicable months later. Its purpose is to ensure that a schedule is a defensible artefact with a provenance, not a number that appeared in a tool.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `Planning Scheduling` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It applies wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired at runtime. It does not govern execution dispatch, decision authority, or reasoning strategy, which are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** scheduling invariants, declared inputs and their freezing rules, determinism and seeds, unschedulable reporting, algorithm classes and degradation, schedule stability and churn budgets, and the scheduling run receipt.

**Out of scope:** prioritisation, which determines the order preference and belongs to Section 28; queueing of execution work, which belongs to Section 27; capacity states, which belong to Section 38; and timeline presentation including critical path, which belongs to Section 39.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

Schedules are commitments expressed as dates, and an organisation's credibility rests on whether those dates mean anything. Two properties create that credibility: the schedule must be reproducible, so that anyone can ask why a date is what it is and receive the same answer twice; and it must be stable, so that a small change does not move every date. Without both, teams learn to ignore the schedule and plan privately, which is the failure mode that scheduling software has been producing for four decades.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Engineered as a pure function from a frozen input set to a schedule plus an unschedulable report plus a receipt. Inputs are frozen by digest or snapshot identity at run start, so a run is reproducible by replaying the same identities. Determinism is enforced by requiring explicit tie-breaking and a recorded seed. Stability is measured as churn against the prior schedule and is subject to a declared budget rather than left to chance.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

Scheduling consumes the compiled plan, the resource resolver snapshot, the constraint set, and the priority scores, and produces a schedule that the timeline, roadmap, and milestone sections read. It writes nothing to the plan itself; a schedule is a derived artefact attached to a plan version, which is what allows several schedules to exist for one version under different scenarios.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

An agent may run the scheduler and may propose input changes, but it must not adjust inputs to make a schedule fit a desired date. The specific prohibited behaviour is shortening durations, relaxing constraints, or inflating envelopes in order to eliminate an unschedulable report. When work does not fit, the agent surfaces the unschedulable report with its reasons; the decision to change an input belongs to a human owner and produces its own record.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `Planning Scheduling` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step depends on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts this section names before writing behaviour, and register each in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no downstream core has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Section-specific sequencing.** Build the declarative definitions before the behaviour, and the refusal paths before the accepted paths, so the first thing that works correctly is the thing that says no.

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Failure Library

These are the failures agents actually produce when implementing `Planning Scheduling`. Each entry names the mistake, the reason an agent makes it, and the corrective behaviour.

| Failure | Why an agent does it | Corrective behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| Silently dropping tasks that do not fit | The resulting schedule looks complete and clean | Emit the unschedulable report; a clean schedule that hides work is a lie with a timeline |
| Using unseeded randomness for tie-breaking | Randomness is an easy way to break ties fairly | Use explicit deterministic tie-breaking, or record the seed as a declared input |
| Rescheduling everything on every run | A full recompute is simpler than an incremental one | Measure churn and stay within the budget; anchor unaffected tasks to their prior placements |
| Adjusting durations to remove an infeasibility | It converts a failed run into a successful one | Report the infeasibility; changing an input to fit a desired output is falsification, not scheduling |
| Inventing a field the schema does not define | The agent needs somewhere to put a value and adds a field rather than asking | Propose a schema change with a version bump; never write undeclared fields |
| Weakening a guard to make a test pass | The guard blocks the happy path the agent is building | Fix the input or the design; a weakened guard is a silent constitutional violation |
| Treating a planned document as if it exists | Cross-references look uniform | Check status; planned documents are cited with `Status: Planned` |

**Normative application:** For `Planning Scheduling`, the owning implementation MUST make this failure mode observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.
