### The Core Layer Order

Every planning core belongs to exactly one layer, and seams may only point downward in the order below or sideways into a cross-cutting core. This is the whole dependency rule; everything else in this section enforces it.

| Layer | Cores | May call | May never call |
|---|---|---|---|
| Intake | intake | derivation, cross-cutting | nothing above; no peer |
| Derivation | derivation | evaluation, cross-cutting | intake, or any peer |
| Evaluation | evaluation | commitment, cross-cutting | intake, derivation |
| Commitment | commitment | projection, cross-cutting | intake, derivation, evaluation |
| Projection | projection | cross-cutting only | every layer above it |
| Cross-cutting | policy, evidence, signal | nothing | every layer, including each other |

Cross-cutting cores calling nothing is what keeps them safe to call from anywhere. The moment a policy core calls the evidence core, the graph acquires a path from every layer to every other layer and the order stops meaning anything.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this layer observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Seam Realisation and Split Eligibility

Seams are realised in process today. The declaration records what each seam would become if planning were split across processes, so a split is an evaluation of recorded facts rather than an investigation.

| Realisation | How it is called | Failure classes | Eligibility requirement |
|---|---|---|---|
| In process, not splittable | Typed call behind the seam interface | Declared outcomes only | None; documented as permanent |
| In process, split candidate | Typed call behind the seam interface | Declared outcomes plus a tested timeout path | Projected split latency within the request budget |
| Out of process, synchronous | Request/response over the internal transport | Declared outcomes, timeout, unavailable | Caller retry and degradation behaviour implemented |
| Out of process, asynchronous | Durable message with at-least-once delivery | Declared outcomes, duplicate delivery, lag | Consumer idempotency proven by test |

The reason a split candidate must have its timeout path tested while still in process is that adding the path after the split is done under incident conditions. The cost of writing it early is one test; the cost of writing it late is an outage.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this realisation observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### What May Cross a Seam

Payload discipline is what keeps a seam narrow. The rules below are absolute; each has been violated on systems of this kind with the stated consequence.

| May cross | May never cross | Why |
|---|---|---|
| A declared payload type owned by the seam | An internal domain object of either core | Internal objects couple both sides to each other's evolution |
| A correlation identifier and principal reference | A credential, token, or raw secret | Secrets crossing seams multiply their blast radius with each hop |
| Identifiers and scoped references | The whole request context object | Passing context makes every field a shared dependency |
| Declared outcome values | Implementation exceptions | Exceptions bind the caller to the callee's language and libraries |
| Bounded collections with a declared maximum | Unbounded result sets | An unbounded payload is a memory incident once the seam becomes a hop |
| Version-tagged payloads | Untagged structures | Without a version, a seam cannot be changed while both sides are running |

Each rule reduces the number of reasons two cores must change together, which is the only measure of seam quality that matters.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this payload rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `Internal Interfaces`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** The derivation core needs evidence for a candidate plan. It calls seam `S-INT-04` once with a declared `EvidenceQuery`, receives an `EvidenceBundle` within its one-millisecond budget, and carries the bundle through the rest of the request rather than calling again. The request closes with one seam call recorded against a budget of one.

**Failure.** A change to intake adds a policy check inside a per-item loop. The seam call budget for `S-INT-01` is two per request; a request with forty items records forty calls. The request still completes, the exceedance is signalled with the seam and count named, and the change is identified as a design defect before it reaches a load test.

**Recovery.** The loop is replaced with a single batch policy check. The seam gains a batch payload type with a declared maximum, the per-request count returns to two, and the internal seam record shows the seam back inside its budget with the batch bound stated.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was, without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Execution Stories

**Execution path.** No internal seam reaches execution. The commitment core's only outward path is the single handoff of Section 90, and the seam graph contains no edge from any planning core to any execution component, which the acyclicity check verifies as an absence rather than trusting as a convention.

**Boundary note.** The execution story ends at the handoff contract. Planning publishes an execution-ready artefact and stops; the execution surface owns everything after that point and reports back only as events.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this execution story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Optimization Stories

**Optimization path.** Recording projected split latency alongside in-process latency turned the question `can we extract the evaluation core?` from a two-week spike into a query against the seam record, and identified two seams whose call counts had to fall before any split was worth attempting.

**Boundary note.** Optimization changes how well a candidate scores against a declared objective function; it never changes who is authorised to commit. Selection between competing commitments remains a decision and is recorded as one.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this optimization story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Recovery Stories

**Recovery path.** A refactor accidentally introduces a seam from the projection core back to the evaluation core. The change never reaches an environment: startup validation detects the cycle, prints the path, and refuses to boot in the developer's own test run. Recovery is removing the edge and passing the needed value downward instead, and the seam record for that day shows the boot refusal rather than a production incident.

**Boundary note.** Recovery restores a declared state from stored evidence; it never invents state, never edits history in place, and never resumes an action whose authorisation has expired.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this recovery story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `Internal Interfaces`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs, its correlation identifier, and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Normative Requirements

Each requirement below is binding for `Internal Interfaces` and is paired with the evidence that demonstrates compliance.

| Requirement ID | Title | Normative statement | Compliance evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R01` | Declared seams only | A cross-core call MUST pass through a declared seam, and any import bypassing one MUST fail the build. | Import boundary check runs as a build gate and names both packages on violation. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R02` | Acyclic downward graph | The seam graph MUST be acyclic and MUST contain no edge pointing upward in the layer order, verified at startup. | Startup validation refuses boot and prints the offending path. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R03` | Declared payload types | Only declared, version-tagged payload types MAY cross a seam; internal domain objects and request contexts MUST NOT. | Seam interface signatures accept declared types only; review checks payload declarations. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R04` | Declared error contract | Every seam MUST declare its closed error set, and no implementation exception MAY escape across a seam. | Seam wrapper converts undeclared failures and emits a signal naming them. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R05` | Call and payload budgets | Every seam MUST declare a per-request call budget and a payload field budget, and exceedances MUST be recorded. | Request close compares observed counts to budgets and writes the seam record. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R06` | Callee-side caching only | Seam results MUST NOT be cached by the caller; per-request reuse MUST be by carrying the value in the request context. | Review check and a test asserting one seam call per request for reused values. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R07` | Tested timeout path for split candidates | A seam marked as a split candidate MUST have a caller timeout and degradation path exercised by a test before it is eligible to be split. | Fault injection suite covering every split candidate seam. |
| `CAT-PE-P4-78-R08` | No orphan cores | Every core except the entry core MUST have at least one inbound seam. | Startup validation refuses boot when a core has no inbound seam. |

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this requirement observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Extension

Part 4 extends the planning constitution established in Part 1 Section 3 and continued by Parts 2 and 3, which together contain rules `CAT-PE-CONST-001` through `CAT-PE-CONST-077`. This section contributes exactly one new rule, continuing the catalogue from `CAT-PE-CONST-078` as the Part 3 handoff requires. It adds a final architecture obligation; it does not weaken any existing rule.

**Rule ID:** `CAT-PE-CONST-080`  
**Title:** Narrow internal seams  
**Normative statement:** Every call between planning cores MUST pass through a declared seam with a stated direction, version-tagged payload type, closed error contract, and per-request call budget; the seam graph MUST remain acyclic with no edge pointing upward in the layer order; and no core MAY import another core's internals directly.  
**Rationale:** Internal seams have no external consumer to complain when they widen, so they widen silently until the system can no longer be split, tested in parts, or understood in parts. Declaring seams as data with budgets converts an aesthetic preference for modularity into a property the build and the boot sequence can verify.  
**Enforcement point:** Build-time import boundary checking, startup graph validation for cycles and upward edges, typed seam interfaces, and per-request call budget measurement.  
**Violation behavior:** The build fails naming both packages, or boot is refused printing the cycle or upward edge, or the request completes with a recorded budget exceedance naming the seam.  
**Validation method:** Automated tests asserting that a bypassing import fails the build, that a synthetic cycle prevents boot, and that an over-budget request writes a seam record with the observed count.  
**Owner:** Lead Repository Architect  
**Related Parts 1 to 3 rules:** `CAT-PE-CONST-067` (structural isolation), `CAT-PE-CONST-079` (versioned public surface), and `CAT-PE-CONST-084` (declared placement).

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this constitutional rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C01 — Declared seams only

- **Rule:** A cross-core call MUST pass through a declared seam, and any import bypassing one MUST fail the build.
- **Business test:** A reviewer confirms this holds by inspecting one real object of this section without asking anyone.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Import boundary check runs as a build gate and names both packages on violation.
- **AI behavior:** The agent verifies this condition before proposing a write and reports the result in the change description.
- **Human boundary:** A human MAY waive this only with a recorded, expiring waiver from Lead Repository Architect.
- **Security assertion:** Violation widens exposure or removes an audit guarantee, so the check fails closed.
- **Performance assertion:** The check is local to the object and its direct references and stays inside the section write budget.
- **Evidence:** `internal seam record`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P4_78_C01`
- **Recovery:** Supply the missing element and retry, or supersede the stored version with a recorded reason.
- **Implementation test:** Automated test asserting both the accepted path and the refused path for this rule.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C09 — Contain: Direct import bypassing a seam

- **Rule:** When `direct import bypassing a seam` is detected, the containment action MUST be build fails with both packages named
- **Business test:** The organisation learns about this failure from a signal rather than from a customer.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Detection signal: Import boundary check finds a cross-core internal import. Containment is executed by the owning core, not by an operator following a runbook from memory.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT suppress, retry past, or reinterpret this condition; it reports and stops.
- **Human boundary:** Lead Repository Architect is accountable for the containment action and its record.
- **Security assertion:** An uncontained failure of this kind leaves the system in a state whose authorisation properties are unknown.
- **Performance assertion:** Detection is continuous and adds a bounded per-operation cost; containment is bounded by the affected object set.
- **Evidence:** `internal seam record`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P4_78_C09`
- **Recovery:** Execute the containment action, write the recovery receipt, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Failure injection test triggering the condition and asserting the declared containment, not merely the absence of a crash.
- **Ownership:** Lead Repository Architect
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Internal Interfaces` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C17 — Security property upheld

- **Rule:** The security property stated by this section MUST hold in the implementation, not only in the prose.
- **Business test:** The property is stated in the operating contract and is checkable against a running system.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Implementation asserts the property in an automated test and emits the corresponding signal. Property: Seams carry authorisation context but never authorisation decisions. A calling core passes the resolved principal and grant context in the payload envelope; the called core re-checks any grant it needs rather than trusting that the caller checked. Internal seams are not a trust boundary in the network sense but are a trust boundary in the correctness sense: a core that assumes its callers validated their input is a core that becomes exploitable the moment a new caller appears. Payloads crossing seams carry no credentials and no raw secrets, only scoped references resolved by the owning core.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT trade this property away for throughput or convenience.
- **Human boundary:** Lead Repository Architect approves any deviation, recorded with an expiry.
- **Security assertion:** The property is part of this section's posture and fails closed when unverifiable.
- **Performance assertion:** Verification is bounded by the object under evaluation, not by portfolio size.
- **Evidence:** `internal seam record`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P4_78_C17`
- **Recovery:** Restore the property, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Automated property test executed in continuous integration.
- **Ownership:** Lead Repository Architect
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Internal Interfaces` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C18 — Consistency property upheld

- **Rule:** The consistency property stated by this section MUST hold in the implementation, not only in the prose.
- **Business test:** The property is stated in the operating contract and is checkable against a running system.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Implementation asserts the property in an automated test and emits the corresponding signal. Property: Within a single request, a value read across a seam is read once and carried, so the request cannot observe two different versions of the same fact. Across requests, seams carry no consistency promise beyond that of the owning core, and a caller that requires a consistent multi-core view requests a snapshot from the projection core rather than assembling one from several seam calls.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT trade this property away for throughput or convenience.
- **Human boundary:** Lead Repository Architect approves any deviation, recorded with an expiry.
- **Security assertion:** The property is part of this section's posture and fails closed when unverifiable.
- **Performance assertion:** Verification is bounded by the object under evaluation, not by portfolio size.
- **Evidence:** `internal seam record`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P4_78_C18`
- **Recovery:** Restore the property, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Automated property test executed in continuous integration.
- **Ownership:** Lead Repository Architect
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Internal Interfaces` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C19 — Recovery property upheld

- **Rule:** The recovery property stated by this section MUST hold in the implementation, not only in the prose.
- **Business test:** The property is stated in the operating contract and is checkable against a running system.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Implementation asserts the property in an automated test and emits the corresponding signal. Property: Seam-level recovery is the caller's declared behaviour for each error in the seam's error contract: retry with backoff, degrade with a marked result, or refuse. These are chosen at declaration time and implemented before the seam carries load, so a seam that later becomes a network call already behaves correctly when the network fails. Recovery of the seam graph itself is redeployment; the graph is data, validated at startup, and a graph that fails validation prevents boot rather than degrading quietly.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT trade this property away for throughput or convenience.
- **Human boundary:** Lead Repository Architect approves any deviation, recorded with an expiry.
- **Security assertion:** The property is part of this section's posture and fails closed when unverifiable.
- **Performance assertion:** Verification is bounded by the object under evaluation, not by portfolio size.
- **Evidence:** `internal seam record`
- **Failure code:** `CAT_PE_P4_78_C19`
- **Recovery:** Restore the property, then re-run the section's acceptance tests before resuming.
- **Implementation test:** Automated property test executed in continuous integration.
- **Ownership:** Lead Repository Architect
- **Constitutional assertion:** This control is binding for `Internal Interfaces` and MUST NOT be weakened without a superseding ADR.

- **Business test:** An auditor finds the receipt for any accepted action without asking an engineer.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Record writer runs inside the same transaction as the accepted write.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT add a write path that bypasses the record writer.

#### CAT-PE-P4-78-C21 — Ownership resolves to a role

- **Rule:** Every owner, approver, and escalation target named by this section MUST resolve to a role in `context/05_AGENTS.md`.
- **Business test:** Escalation never depends on knowing which individual to call.
- **Engineering enforcement:** Startup validation refuses to boot when a named role does not resolve.
- **AI behavior:** The agent MUST NOT name an individual where a role is required.
- **Human boundary:** Lead Repository Architect maintains the role bindings for this section.
- **Security assertion:** Unresolvable ownership breaks accountability, so the binding check fails closed.

### Acceptance Tests

The acceptance tests below MUST pass before any implementation of `Internal Interfaces` is considered complete.

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-001`  
**Purpose:** Bypassing imports fail the build  
**Given:** A source file importing another core's internal package  
**When:** The build runs  
**Then:** The build fails naming the importing and imported packages  
**Failure condition:** The build succeeds with a cross-core internal import present

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-002`  
**Purpose:** Cycles prevent boot  
**Given:** A seam declaration set containing a cycle  
**When:** The engine starts  
**Then:** Boot is refused and the cycle path is printed  
**Failure condition:** The engine boots with a cyclic seam graph

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-003`  
**Purpose:** Upward edges prevent boot  
**Given:** A seam whose callee layer is above its caller layer  
**When:** The engine starts  
**Then:** Boot is refused with the seam identifier named  
**Failure condition:** An upward seam is accepted at startup

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-004`  
**Purpose:** Seams without error contracts prevent boot  
**Given:** A seam declaration with an empty error contract  
**When:** The engine starts  
**Then:** Boot is refused with the seam identifier named  
**Failure condition:** A seam with no declared failures is accepted

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-005`  
**Purpose:** Undeclared failures are converted and signalled  
**Given:** A callee raising an exception outside its error contract  
**When:** The seam wrapper handles it  
**Then:** A declared outcome is returned and a signal names the undeclared failure  
**Failure condition:** The raw exception reaches the caller

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-006`  
**Purpose:** Call budget exceedance is recorded  
**Given:** A seam with a budget of two called four times in one request  
**When:** The request closes  
**Then:** A seam record is written with the seam, observed count, and budget  
**Failure condition:** The exceedance completes without a record

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-007`  
**Purpose:** Internal objects cannot cross a seam  
**Given:** A call passing an internal domain object  
**When:** The seam is invoked  
**Then:** The call is rejected as a payload type mismatch  
**Failure condition:** The internal object crosses the seam

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-008`  
**Purpose:** Cores without inbound seams prevent boot  
**Given:** A declared core with no inbound seam and which is not the entry core  
**When:** The engine starts  
**Then:** Boot is refused with the core named  
**Failure condition:** An unreachable core is accepted at startup

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-009`  
**Purpose:** Split candidates have tested timeout paths  
**Given:** A seam marked as a split candidate  
**When:** The eligibility check runs  
**Then:** A fault injection test covering timeout is required and its absence blocks the mark  
**Failure condition:** A split candidate is marked with no timeout coverage

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-010`  
**Purpose:** Cross-cutting cores call nothing  
**Given:** A seam from one cross-cutting core to another  
**When:** The engine starts  
**Then:** Boot is refused with both cores named  
**Failure condition:** Cross-cutting cores are allowed to call each other

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-011`  
**Purpose:** Per-request values are read once  
**Given:** A value used five times within one request  
**When:** The request completes  
**Then:** Exactly one seam call is recorded for that value  
**Failure condition:** The seam is called once per use

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S78-012`  
**Purpose:** Payload field budgets are enforced at review  
**Given:** A payload type exceeding its declared field budget  
**When:** The seam width review runs  
**Then:** The seam is reported over budget with the observed field count  
**Failure condition:** The widened payload passes review unreported

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this acceptance test observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Future Evolution

`Internal Interfaces` evolves in three predictable directions. First, seam declarations generate their interfaces in every supported language, so a core rewritten in Go or Rust inherits the same contract without a translation step. Second, projected split latency becomes continuously computed from production measurement rather than estimated, making split eligibility a live property. Third, seam width trends become a governance signal, so a seam that has grown three fields in a quarter is reviewed before it grows a fourth.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this evolution path observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### 2030 to 2035 Continuities

The following properties of `Internal Interfaces` are expected to hold through 2035 regardless of implementation technology: role-based ownership, append-only history, evidence-backed completion, deny-by-default access, and a hard boundary against execution. Technologies, languages, and storage engines will change; these five properties are what make planning content written in 2026 still interpretable and still trustworthy in 2035. For internal interfaces specifically, the durable property is that dependency direction must be verifiable by a machine. Languages, frameworks, and deployment topologies will all change; a codebase whose dependency rules are checked at every build will still be decomposable in 2035, and one that relies on reviewers noticing will have become a single unit that nobody can safely divide.

**Normative application:** For `Internal Interfaces`, the owning implementation MUST make this continuity observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

## 79. Event Model

**Section ID:** `CAT-PE-P4-79`  
**Constitutional domain:** Planning event publication  
**Human accountable owner:** Planning Contract Owner  
**Primary record:** `event contract record`  
**Decision status:** Final architecture clause set; completes Parts 1 to 3 without weakening them.  
**Primary question:** What facts does planning publish, what shape and ordering do they carry, and why is an event never an instruction?

### Purpose

This section defines the event model of the planning engine: the closed set of facts planning publishes, the envelope every one of them carries, the ordering and delivery guarantees consumers may rely on, and the absolute rule that a planning event states what happened rather than what someone should do next. Events are the widest interface a system has, because any consumer may subscribe and the publisher rarely learns who did. The purpose here is to make that interface as safe as its reach demands: fact-shaped, versioned, ordered where ordering is promised, and free of any authority to cause action.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this purpose observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scope

This section governs `Event Model` for every planning core, contract, record, and interface in the CAT repository. It applies wherever planning content is created, derived, validated, stored, transitioned, read, or retired at runtime. It does not govern execution dispatch, decision authority, or reasoning strategy, which are reached only through declared contracts.

**In scope:** the closed planning event catalogue; the common event envelope; ordering, delivery, and retention guarantees; schema versioning and compatibility for events; consumer registration and replay; the distinction between a fact and an instruction; and the event contract record.

**Out of scope:** the transport and broker configuration, which belongs to `context/08_EVENTS_SYSTEM.md`; commands, which are Section 80; queries and projections, which are Section 81; the handoff to execution, which is Section 90; and audit records, which are Section 98.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this boundary observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Business Explanation

Events are how the rest of the organisation learns what planning did without asking. A clear event catalogue means a reporting team, a finance integration, and an operations dashboard can each build independently and none of them needs a change from the planning team. The commercial risk is the opposite condition: events shaped as instructions, which make consumers into hidden parts of the planning system and turn every consumer change into a planning incident.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this business outcome observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Engineering Explanation

Every planning event carries one envelope: event identifier, event type, type version, subject identity, occurrence time, recording time, correlation identifier, causation identifier, producer, sequence number within its subject, tenant, and payload. Events are published only after the state they describe is durably committed, using the transactional outbox pattern so that no event describes a state that was rolled back and no committed state fails to produce its event. Payloads are additive-only within a version; a change that removes or reinterprets a field publishes a new event type version alongside the existing one.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this engineering behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Architecture Explanation

Architecturally, events are the only outbound channel that fans out. Commands come in, queries read projections, and events go out to an unbounded set of consumers planning does not know. That asymmetry drives every rule here: because the publisher cannot negotiate with consumers, it must never depend on them, must never assume any of them acted, and must never encode an expectation of action in the payload. Planning's own projections consume the same event stream as everyone else, which keeps the stream honest, because a stream that is insufficient for external consumers would first be insufficient for planning itself.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this architectural position observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Explanation

The characteristic agent failure here is publishing an event named for what should happen next. `PlanNeedsApproval` and `ExecutionShouldStart` read naturally and are both instructions wearing the costume of a fact. The facts are `PlanSubmittedForApproval` and `PlanCommitted`; what a consumer does with either is the consumer's decision. An agent must also never add a field to an event because one consumer asked for it in a support conversation, because every field published becomes a field every consumer may come to depend on.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this agent behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Implementation Strategy

Implementation of `Event Model` proceeds in a fixed order so that each step produces evidence the next step depends on. The order is not a preference; skipping a step produces a core that cannot prove its own correctness.

1. **Model first.** Define the objects, records, and contracts this section names before writing behaviour, and register each in the schema registry with a version.
2. **Validate at the boundary.** Reject invalid content at the contract layer so no downstream core has to defend itself against malformed planning content.
3. **Version everything.** Every schema, machine, rule set, and object carries a version, and every change supersedes rather than overwrites.
4. **Observe continuously.** Emit the signals named in this section from the first commit, not after the first incident.
5. **Fail closed.** When a check cannot complete, refuse and record the refusal rather than proceeding on an assumption.

**Section-specific sequencing.** Define the event type and its envelope before the code that emits it, write the outbox and the ordering guarantee before the first consumer exists, and publish the schema before the first event, so no consumer ever receives a fact whose contract is not already fixed.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this strategy observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Implementation Blueprint

### AI Failure Library

|---|---|---|
| Naming an event for the action it expects | `ExecutionShouldStart` describes the intent clearly | Name events for what happened; an instruction disguised as a fact creates hidden coupling |

| Adding a field to an existing event version | The addition is backward compatible | Additive fields are permitted only when declared optional in the schema; anything else is a new version |
| Assuming a consumer processed an event | The event was published successfully | Publication is not consumption; planning never depends on a consumer having acted |
| Inventing a field the schema does not define | The agent needs somewhere to put a value and adds a field rather than asking | Propose a schema change with a version bump; never write undeclared fields |
| Weakening a guard to make a test pass | The guard blocks the happy path the agent is building | Fix the input or the design; a weakened guard is a silent constitutional violation |
| Treating a planned document as if it exists | Cross-references look uniform | Check status; planned documents are cited with `Status: Planned` |

### Security

Event payloads carry identifiers and classifications rather than sensitive content; a consumer that needs protected detail resolves it through an authorised query, where the grant is checked against that consumer. Subscriptions are authorised per consumer and per tenant, and topic partitioning enforces tenant separation so a cross-tenant read is structurally impossible rather than filtered out. Events are signed by the producer so a consumer can verify origin, and no event ever carries a credential, a token, or free-text that has not passed the same redaction rules as logs.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this security property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Performance

The event path is measured from state commit to broker acknowledgement, with a budget of two hundred milliseconds at the ninety-fifth percentile, and separately from broker acknowledgement to projection application. Outbox relay is batched and its backlog is a first-class signal, because a growing outbox means the system's public account of itself is falling behind its actual state, which is a correctness problem long before it is a performance one.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this performance property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Latency

Planning's own projections apply events within one second at the ninety-fifth percentile, and that figure is what Section 81 discloses as query lag. External consumer latency is not planning's promise and is not measured as such; what planning promises is the time from commit to publication, which is the only part it controls.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this latency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Scalability

Topics are partitioned by subject identity, so throughput scales with partition count while per-subject ordering is preserved. Consumers scale independently and their lag is their own concern; planning's publication rate is bounded by its commit rate, not by the slowest consumer. The event boundary therefore decouples planning's scale from the aggregate scale of everything that watches it, which is the property that makes hundreds of consumers viable.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this scalability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Reliability and Availability

Delivery is at least once, ordered per subject, and consumers are required to be idempotent; this is stated in the contract rather than left as an implementation detail, because a consumer that assumes exactly-once will eventually double-count. The outbox guarantees that every committed change produces its event, and reconciliation between committed changes and published events runs continuously so a gap is detected rather than inferred later from a consumer complaint.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this reliability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Caching

Events are not cached; they are retained. Retention is declared per topic with a minimum window that allows a consumer to rebuild from the stream after an outage of that length. Snapshot topics hold the latest state per subject and may be compacted; fact topics are never compacted within the retention window, because a consumer replaying history must see the same history planning saw.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this caching property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Consistency

The consistency property of this section is that events and state never disagree. The outbox makes publication part of the same transaction as the state change, so there is no window in which a state exists without its event or an event exists without its state. Across subjects there is no global ordering and none is promised; a consumer that needs a cross-subject view builds it from a projection with a declared lag rather than assuming the stream is globally ordered.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this consistency property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Recovery Strategy

Recovery for consumers is replay from a recorded offset within the retention window, which is why retention length and rebuild time are declared together. Recovery for publication is outbox drain: entries remain until acknowledged, so a broker outage delays events without losing them. Recovery from a defective event type is a corrective event of a new version, never a deletion or an in-place amendment, because consumers have already acted on what they received and an erased fact cannot be un-acted.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this recovery property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Monitoring and Observability

Observability for `Event Model` is defined by its failure modes: every failure mode has a detection signal, and every detection signal is emitted by the implementation rather than inferred by an operator. A failure mode with no signal is an unmonitored failure mode and is treated as a gap.

- **Counters:** events published by type and version, outbox entries written and relayed, publication failures, reconciliation gaps detected, consumer registrations by topic, replay requests served, schema validation rejections at publish.
- **Gauges:** outbox backlog depth, oldest unrelayed outbox entry age, event types by version, consumers on deprecated event versions, retention window remaining per topic.
- **Histograms:** commit-to-publish latency, publish-to-projection latency, event payload sizes by type, replay durations by consumer.
- **Traces:** one span per blueprint stage, correlated by plan identity and correlation identifier.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this signal observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Runtime Behaviour

At runtime a state change and its outbox entry commit together. The relay reads unsent outbox entries in order, publishes them to the partition determined by subject identity, and marks them sent only on broker acknowledgement. Each event carries the full envelope, including a per-subject sequence number that consumers use to detect gaps and duplicates. A reconciliation job compares committed state changes against published events continuously and raises a signal naming any change without a corresponding event. Every publication cycle contributes to the event contract record.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this runtime behaviour observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Maintainability

Maintainability of `Event Model` depends on keeping declarations declarative: schemas, machines, rules, and grants are data, compiled and validated at startup, so a change is reviewed as a diff of intent rather than a diff of conditionals scattered across services. Every declaration is versioned, and a version is retired only when no live object is pinned to it. For events specifically, maintainability means being able to add a consumer without asking anyone. That is only true when the catalogue, the schemas, and the retention windows are published and accurate, so keeping them generated from one source is the whole maintenance strategy.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this maintainability property observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Extension Points

`Event Model` is extended by adding declarations, never by editing behaviour in place. A new event type is added by declaring it in the catalogue with its subject kind, payload schema, ordering guarantee, and retention window, and by emitting it from the outbox alongside its state change. An existing type is extended only with optional fields declared as such in its schema; a removal or reinterpretation is a new version published alongside the old one until every registered consumer has moved. Any extension that changes an existing declaration's meaning is a superseding version, not an extension.

### Risks

| Risk | Impact if unmanaged | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Events drift into instructions | Consumers become hidden components of planning and every consumer change is a planning incident | Catalogue review rejects action-named types; the naming rule is a documented gate |
| Payloads grow to satisfy individual consumers | Every field becomes a promise and the stream becomes a shared mutable model | Payloads carry identifiers and classifications; detail is resolved by authorised query |
| Consumers assume exactly-once delivery | Duplicates cause double-counting that surfaces as a data quality incident months later | At-least-once is stated in the contract and duplicate delivery is exercised in consumer contract tests |
| Retention is set by storage cost rather than rebuild time | A consumer outage longer than retention becomes unrecoverable | Retention is declared as the maximum of measured rebuild time and the stated outage tolerance |

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this risk observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Anti-patterns

- **Events that carry the full entity on every change.** Consumers begin treating the stream as their database and the publisher can never change a field again.
- **A single topic for all planning events.** Ordering, retention, and authorisation then apply uniformly to facts that need different treatment.
- **Deleting or amending a published event.** Consumers have already acted; rewriting history makes the audit account unreconstructable.
- **Relying on a global event order.** It does not exist in a partitioned stream, and code that assumes it fails intermittently under load.
- **Publishing an event to trigger planning's own next step.** It turns an external boundary into an internal control flow whose latency and delivery are outside planning's control.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this prohibition observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Best Practices

- Name every event for the fact that occurred, in the past tense, never for a desired action.
- Publish from a transactional outbox after commit, never before it.
- Carry one envelope on every event, including correlation, causation, and per-subject sequence.
- Partition by subject identity and promise ordering only within a subject.
- State at-least-once delivery in the contract and require consumer idempotency.
- Keep payloads to identifiers, classifications, and the minimum facts consumers need.
- Set retention from measured rebuild time, not from storage convenience.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this practice observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Counter Examples

A team publishes planning events directly from the service method before the transaction commits, uses one topic for everything, names types after what consumers should do, and includes the full plan entity in every payload because `then consumers do not need to call us`. Six months later a rolled-back transaction has produced a downstream purchase, and no field of the plan entity can be renamed.

The following configuration is rejected by the guards described in this section:

```json
{
  "object": "rejected_event_model_configuration",
  "section": "CAT-PE-P4-79",
  "submitted": {
    "publication": "direct_from_service_method_pre_commit",
    "topics": "single_topic_for_all_events",
    "naming": [
      "ExecutionShouldStart",
      "PlanNeedsApproval"
    ],
    "payload": "full_plan_entity_on_every_change",
    "ordering_claim": "global",
    "delivery_claim": "exactly_once",
    "retention_days": 3,
    "corrections": "delete_and_republish"
  },
  "errors": []
}
```

- **Rejected:** Publishing before commit lets an event describe a state that never existed.
- **Rejected:** A single topic forces one retention, one ordering, and one authorisation on unrelated facts.
- **Rejected:** Action-named types make consumers hidden components of the planning system.
- **Rejected:** Full-entity payloads freeze the internal model into a public contract.
- **Rejected:** Global ordering does not exist in a partitioned stream and code depending on it fails under load.
- **Rejected:** Claiming exactly-once delivery guarantees consumers will omit idempotency and double-count.
- **Rejected:** Three days of retention is shorter than any realistic consumer rebuild.
- **Rejected:** Deleting and republishing rewrites history that consumers have already acted upon.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this rejection observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Pseudo Code

The logic below is complete for the behaviour it describes; it contains no omission markers and can be transliterated into any of the languages named in Section 5.

```text
CATALOGUE = load_event_catalogue()

function emit(change, event_type, payload, context):
    entry = CATALOGUE.find(event_type)
    if entry is absent:
        return refuse("undeclared_event_type", event_type)
    if is_action_named(event_type):
        return refuse("instruction_shaped_event", event_type)
    if not validate_schema(payload, entry.current_schema):
        return refuse("payload_schema_invalid", event_type)
    if contains_protected_content(payload):
        return refuse("protected_content_in_payload", event_type)

    envelope = {
        "event_id": new_event_id(),
        "event_type": event_type,
        "type_version": entry.current_version,
        "subject_kind": entry.subject_kind,
        "subject_id": change.subject_id,
        "occurred_at": change.occurred_at,
        "recorded_at": now(),
        "correlation_id": context.correlation_id,
        "causation_id": context.causation_id,
        "producer": producer_identity(),
        "sequence_in_subject": next_sequence(change.subject_id),
        "tenant": change.tenant,
        "payload": payload,
    }

    # state change and outbox entry share one transaction
    with transaction() as tx:
        tx.apply(change)
        tx.insert_outbox(envelope)
    return envelope.event_id

function relay():
    batch = outbox.read_unsent(limit=500, ordered_by="sequence")
    for envelope in batch:
        entry = CATALOGUE.find(envelope.event_type)
        partition = partition_for(envelope.subject_id, entry.topic)
        ack = broker.publish(entry.topic, partition, sign(envelope))
        if ack.ok:
            outbox.mark_sent(envelope.event_id, ack.offset)
        else:
            emit_signal("publication_failed", envelope.event_type, ack.reason)
            break                      # preserve order; retry from here
    report_gauge("outbox_backlog", outbox.unsent_count())
    report_gauge("oldest_unrelayed_age_s", outbox.oldest_unsent_age())
    return "relayed"

function reconcile(window):
    changes = state_log.changes_in(window)
    published = event_log.events_in(window)
    for change in changes:
        if published.none_matching(change.change_id):
            emit_signal("committed_change_without_event", change.change_id)
            outbox.repair_from_change(change)
    for event in published:
        if changes.none_matching(event.causation_change_id):
            emit_signal("event_without_committed_change", event.event_id)
    return "reconciled"

function correct(event_id, reason):
    # never delete, never amend
    original = event_log.get(event_id)
    corrective = build_corrective_event(original, reason)
    return emit(corrective.change, original.event_type + ".corrected",
                corrective.payload, corrective.context)
```

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this algorithm observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Fact Versus Instruction

Every rejected event name below was proposed on a system of this kind. The distinction is not stylistic: an instruction-shaped event makes the publisher responsible for the consumer's behaviour, which is exactly the coupling events exist to avoid.

| Rejected name | Why it is an instruction | Accepted fact | Who decides next |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ExecutionShouldStart` | States what another system must do | `planning.plan.committed` | The execution surface |
| `PlanNeedsApproval` | Encodes an obligation on a human | `planning.plan.submitted_for_approval` | The approving role |
| `NotifyPortfolioOwner` | Names a channel and a recipient | `planning.constraint.breached` | The notification service |
| `RetryEvidenceFetch` | Directs internal control flow over the bus | `planning.evidence.fetch_failed` | The derivation core |
| `ArchivePlan` | Commands a downstream lifecycle action | `planning.plan.superseded` | The retention owner |

The test is simple. If removing every consumer would make the event pointless, it is an instruction. A fact remains true and worth recording even when nobody is listening.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this naming rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Guarantees Consumers May Rely On

Consumers build against the guarantees below and nothing else. Anything not listed here is explicitly not promised, and code that depends on it is unsupported.

| Guarantee | Scope | What is promised | What is not promised |
|---|---|---|---|
| Delivery | Per subscription | At least once within the retention window | Exactly once; consumers must be idempotent |
| Ordering | Per subject identity | Monotonic sequence numbers with no gaps | Any ordering across subjects or topics |
| Durability | Per topic | Retained for the declared window regardless of consumption | Retention beyond the window for slow consumers |
| Completeness | Per committed change | Every committed change produces its event | That every event has been consumed |
| Immutability | Per published event | Never amended, never deleted within retention | That later corrective events will not change the interpretation |
| Freshness | Per publication | Commit to publish within two hundred milliseconds at p95 | Time to reach any particular consumer |

The completeness guarantee deserves emphasis. Planning promises that its account of itself is complete; it promises nothing about whether anyone read it, and it never waits to find out.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this guarantee observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Event Type Version Transitions

Event schemas change. The transitions below are the only permitted ones, and each states what happens to consumers that have not moved.

| Change | Permitted | Mechanism | Effect on existing consumers |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add an optional field | Yes | Same version, schema marks it optional | None; strict parsers must ignore unknown optional fields |
| Add a required field | No | New type version published alongside | None until they subscribe to the new version |
| Remove a field | No | New type version published alongside | None until they subscribe to the new version |
| Change a field's meaning | No | New type version with a differently named field | None; the old field keeps its original meaning forever |
| Rename an event type | No | New type published; old type deprecated | Both are published during the overlap window |
| Retire a version | Yes, after sunset | Deprecation signalled on the catalogue and to registered consumers | Registered consumers are contacted before the sunset date |

Publishing two versions of the same fact during an overlap window costs storage and a small amount of relay work. Breaking a consumer costs their trust, which is not recoverable at any price.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this version transition observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Operational Stories

Four story types are recorded for `Event Model`: a normal-path story, a failure story, a recovery story, and an audit story. Together they describe what this section looks like in operation.

**Normal path.** A plan commits. The state change and its outbox entry commit in one transaction; the relay publishes `planning.plan.committed` version three to the plan facts topic within ninety-six milliseconds, partitioned by plan identity with sequence number fourteen. Three consumers receive it, and planning never learns which of them acted.

**Failure.** A broker partition becomes unavailable. The relay halts on that partition to preserve order, the outbox backlog gauge rises, and the oldest unrelayed entry age crosses its threshold within four minutes. Planning continues committing state; no event is lost and none is published out of order.

**Recovery.** The partition returns. The relay drains the backlog in sequence, consumers receive the delayed events with their original occurrence times intact, and the event contract record for the day states the maximum publication lag observed rather than presenting the period as normal.

**Audit.** An auditor reconstructs the sequence from the records this section writes, confirming who acted, under which rule set version, with which evidence, and what the outcome was, without asking anyone what happened.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this operational story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Execution Stories

**Execution path.** No event causes execution. `planning.plan.committed` states that a plan was committed; the execution surface subscribes and decides for itself, and the actual handoff of an execution-ready artefact remains the single boundary crossing of Section 90. An event that attempted to start execution would be rejected at catalogue review as instruction-shaped.

**Boundary note.** The execution story ends at the handoff contract. Planning publishes an execution-ready artefact and stops; the execution surface owns everything after that point and reports back only as events.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this execution story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Optimization Stories

**Optimization path.** Moving from per-row publication to batched outbox relay reduced broker round trips by a factor of twelve and cut commit-to-publish latency at the ninety-fifth percentile from three hundred and forty milliseconds to ninety-six, while preserving per-subject order because batches are relayed in sequence.

**Boundary note.** Optimization changes how well a candidate scores against a declared objective function; it never changes who is authorised to commit. Selection between competing commitments remains a decision and is recorded as one.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this optimization story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Recovery Stories

**Recovery path.** A consumer discovers it mis-processed two days of a fact type after a bug in its own code. It requests replay from its recorded offset, which lies inside the ninety-day retention window, and reprocesses idempotently. Planning does nothing special: no event is re-emitted, no history is altered, and the replay appears in the record as a served replay request rather than as an incident.

**Boundary note.** Recovery restores a declared state from stored evidence; it never invents state, never edits history in place, and never resumes an action whose authorisation has expired.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this recovery story observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### End-to-End Constitutional Procedure

The procedure below is the full constitutional path for `Event Model`, from request to evidence. It is the sequence auditors replay.

1. The requesting role submits the action with its inputs, its correlation identifier, and its claimed authority.
2. The contract layer validates structure, references, tenancy, and metadata completeness.
3. The section's guards evaluate in order, each producing a pass or a named refusal reason.
4. On refusal the reason is recorded, the caller is informed, and processing stops with nothing stored.
5. On pass the new version is appended, never updated in place, with a monotonic version number.
6. The receipt named by this section is written and linked to the version digest.
7. A fact is published to the event boundary for consumers that do not need to block.
8. Projections rebuild and publish their lag, making the change visible to grant-holding roles.
9. The action becomes replayable: any auditor can recompute the outcome from stored inputs alone.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this procedural step observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Constitutional Extension

Part 4 extends the planning constitution established in Part 1 Section 3 and continued by Parts 2 and 3, which together contain rules `CAT-PE-CONST-001` through `CAT-PE-CONST-077`. This section contributes exactly one new rule, continuing the catalogue from `CAT-PE-CONST-078` as the Part 3 handoff requires. It adds a final architecture obligation; it does not weaken any existing rule.

**Rule ID:** `CAT-PE-CONST-081`  
**Title:** Facts not instructions  
**Normative statement:** Planning MUST publish only declared, fact-named, version-tagged events from a transactional outbox written with the state change they describe; events MUST carry the common envelope with per-subject monotonic sequence, MUST be delivered at least once with ordering promised only within a subject, and MUST NOT instruct any consumer to act or be amended or deleted after publication.  
**Rationale:** Events reach consumers the publisher will never meet, so every property of them must be safe by construction rather than by agreement. Facts published after commit can be trusted; instructions published before commit create actions for states that never existed and make every consumer a hidden part of planning.  
**Enforcement point:** Catalogue validation at startup, naming gate at catalogue review and in CI, outbox-only publication path, continuous change-to-event reconciliation, and an append-only event store.  
**Violation behavior:** The emit call is refused naming the reason, the catalogue change is rejected, or the reconciliation signal names the missing or orphaned record.  
**Validation method:** Automated tests asserting that an undeclared type is refused, that a rolled-back transaction publishes nothing, that per-subject sequence is monotonic under concurrency, and that an amendment attempt is rejected.  
**Owner:** Planning Contract Owner  
**Related Parts 1 to 3 rules:** `CAT-PE-CONST-062` (verifiable history), `CAT-PE-CONST-079` (versioned public surface), and `CAT-PE-CONST-084` (one source of truth).

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this constitutional rule observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### Acceptance Tests

The acceptance tests below MUST pass before any implementation of `Event Model` is considered complete.

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-001`  
**Purpose:** Undeclared event types are refused  
**Given:** An emit call for a type absent from the catalogue  
**When:** The emit path runs  
**Then:** The call is refused with the type named and nothing is written to the outbox  
**Failure condition:** An undeclared type reaches the outbox

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-002`  
**Purpose:** Rolled-back transactions publish nothing  
**Given:** A state change that raises after the outbox insert  
**When:** The transaction rolls back  
**Then:** No outbox entry survives and no event is published  
**Failure condition:** An event describes a rolled-back state

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-003`  
**Purpose:** Committed changes always produce events  
**Given:** A committed change with a declared event type and a suppressed emit  
**When:** Reconciliation runs  
**Then:** The gap is signalled with the change identifier and repaired from the change  
**Failure condition:** The missing event is never detected

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-004`  
**Purpose:** Per-subject sequence is monotonic  
**Given:** Twenty concurrent changes to one subject  
**When:** The events are published  
**Then:** Sequence numbers are contiguous and strictly increasing with no duplicates  
**Failure condition:** A sequence number repeats or a gap appears

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-005`  
**Purpose:** Ordering is preserved under relay retry  
**Given:** A broker rejection in the middle of a relay batch  
**When:** The relay retries  
**Then:** Publication resumes from the failed entry and later entries are not published first  
**Failure condition:** A later event is published before an earlier one for the same subject

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-006`  
**Purpose:** Duplicate delivery is tolerated by contract  
**Given:** The same event delivered twice to a consumer  
**When:** The consumer contract test runs  
**Then:** The consumer's state is identical after one and after two deliveries  
**Failure condition:** The second delivery changes consumer state

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-007`  
**Purpose:** Instruction-shaped names are rejected  
**Given:** A proposed event type named for a required action  
**When:** The catalogue naming check runs  
**Then:** The type is rejected with the fact-shaped alternative suggested  
**Failure condition:** An action-named type enters the catalogue

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-008`  
**Purpose:** Published events cannot be amended  
**Given:** An attempt to update a published event's payload  
**When:** The event store receives the update  
**Then:** The write is rejected as append-only  
**Failure condition:** The stored event changes

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-009`  
**Purpose:** Protected content cannot be published  
**Given:** A payload containing protected content  
**When:** The emit path validates it  
**Then:** The emit is refused and the field is reported  
**Failure condition:** Protected content is published to a topic

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-010`  
**Purpose:** Breaking schema changes are blocked  
**Given:** A schema removing a field from an existing event version  
**When:** The compatibility gate runs  
**Then:** The change is blocked and a new version is required  
**Failure condition:** The removal is deployed under the existing version

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-011`  
**Purpose:** Retention covers measured rebuild time  
**Given:** A measured consumer rebuild of six hours and a declared retention of three hours  
**When:** Retention validation runs  
**Then:** The topic configuration is rejected with both figures reported  
**Failure condition:** Retention shorter than rebuild time is accepted

**Test ID:** `CAT-PE-AT-S79-012`  
**Purpose:** Outbox backlog is observable  
**Given:** A broker outage of ten minutes  
**When:** The relay is blocked  
**Then:** Backlog depth and oldest unrelayed age gauges rise and cross their thresholds  
**Failure condition:** The backlog grows without a signal

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this acceptance test observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### AI Memory Anchor

An agent that retains nothing else from this section retains the following. A closed catalogue of fact-named, version-tagged events published from a transactional outbox with a common envelope, ordered per subject and delivered at least once. No event precedes its commit, no committed change lacks its event, no event instructs a consumer, and no published event is ever changed.

**Memory anchor ID:** `CAT-PE-MEM-S79-001`  
**Concept:** A closed catalogue of fact-named, version-tagged events published from a transactional outbox with a common envelope, ordered per subject and delivered at least once.  
**Invariant:** No event precedes its commit, no committed change lacks its event, no event instructs a consumer, and no published event is ever changed.  
**Relationship:** This section supplies the stream Section 81 projects, Section 82 synchronises from, and Section 98 audits; Section 77 exposes it.  
**Implementation implication:** Implementations MUST publish only from the outbox and MUST reconcile committed changes against published events continuously.

**Anchor:** `Event Model` = published facts, committed first, ordered per subject, never amended, governed by Planning event publication, evidenced by `event contract record`, owned by Planning Contract Owner.

### Future Evolution

`Event Model` evolves in three predictable directions. First, the catalogue becomes machine-published so consumers generate their own handlers and schema drift between publisher and consumer disappears. Second, per-consumer dependency reports identify which fields of which versions each registered consumer actually reads, turning deprecation into a targeted conversation. Third, reconciliation between committed changes and published events becomes continuous and externally attestable, so the completeness guarantee is demonstrated rather than asserted.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this evolution path observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.

### 2030 to 2035 Continuities

The following properties of `Event Model` are expected to hold through 2035 regardless of implementation technology: role-based ownership, append-only history, evidence-backed completion, deny-by-default access, and a hard boundary against execution. Technologies, languages, and storage engines will change; these five properties are what make planning content written in 2026 still interpretable and still trustworthy in 2035. For events specifically, the durable property is that a fact, once published, is never rewritten. Brokers, serialisation formats, and delivery semantics will all be replaced between now and 2035; an append-only stream of well-named facts with a stable envelope will still be interpretable after every one of those replacements, and a mutable stream of instructions will not survive the first of them.

**Normative application:** For `Event Model`, the owning implementation MUST make this continuity observable through a named contract, a policy or guard, a test or review check, and an operational signal. A prose claim without enforcement evidence is incomplete.
